#1036. Enzo Maresca finds the key to Elliot Anderson’s brilliance but Man City still flounder

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Manchester City 1-1 Fulham: Enzo Maresca’s side have picked up just one point in their last four outings but Anderson’s performance offered a silver lining

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

A £116m transfer fee would automatically place anyone under the spotlight. Of late, it has appeared that Elliot Anderson has assumed a prominence anyway, and not always in ways he would have wished. A first return to Nottingham Forest was notable for the challenge he lost to Xavier Schlager that led to Liam Delap galloping clear to score. A meeting with Spain’s World Cup winners was curtailed by a red card for fouling Lamine Yamal; naively, really, given it brought the dual punishments of a dismissal and a penalty.

So if it is safe to say Manchester City needed Anderson’s equaliser against Fulham, it feels equally true that he did. “Nice moment for him, nice moment for us,” said Enzo Maresca. City were facing up to the prospect of a fourth straight league defeat. Anderson’s first top-flight goal since an extraordinarily expensive move averted that.

It offered an illustration of his considerable qualities – and, his mishap at the City Ground notwithstanding, Anderson has been one of City’s finest players in their decidedly mixed season – as well as an idea of how best to deploy them. “We used him today for the first time since the season started as an attacking midfielder,” Maresca explained.

A problem for much of this season is that Anderson has seemed to be playing centre midfield on his own which, even for a player who commanded a nine-figure fee, posed certain difficulties when he was outnumbered. It had felt all the more needless when City’s midfield rebuild came at a record cost.

With Enzo Fernandez reduced to a cameo, his wanderlust taking him to the bench, and Ayyoub Bouaddi starting, Anderson had a partner. “Ayyoub and Elliot were both really good,” said Maresca. It was not a one-stop solution to bring City solidity: they still conceded, for the 18th occasion in their last nine games, and looked too open. “We need to find a way to keep clean sheets,” Maresca admitted.

But Bouaddi’s presence helped liberate Anderson and there were two moments to demonstrate what he can do when unleashed in the final third. The first was his leveller, a crisp, clean volley from the edge of the box, almost as impressive technically as his strike at the Etihad Stadium for Forest last season. “Fantastic goal,” said Maresca.

It came after Fulham had cleared a corner so arguably Anderson would have been in the same position if Fernandez was not on the pitch. Not when he almost got a winner, though: eight yards out, angling a shot just wide after linking up with Erling Haaland, following the kind of box-crashing run that players like Ilkay Gundogan and Kevin De Bruyne have made when used as No 8s by City. They have instead tended to be Fernandez’s remit this season.

And if Fernandez is the conundrum, rather than Anderson, there is nevertheless the case that a double act really brings the best out of him. Until his early exit, he excelled alongside Declan Rice in a duo in Madrid. “It has been an interesting week,” said Anderson, which rather underplayed it.

A problem for Maresca is that, even when identifying a way of using Anderson, City still floundered. This was another incoherent display as the longest winning streak between two clubs in English football came to an end. “We knew we lost the last 20 times we played Manchester City but I told [the players] we would have the chance to beat them if we play with courage, with character,” said Alvaro Arbeloa.

Fulham’s first point against City since 2011 was a sign of the progress under the Spaniard, following draws against Liverpool and Manchester United. Arbeloa knocked City out of the Champions League last season when with Real Madrid. He showed his prowess with lesser players as Fulham pressed man-for-man, played a variant of 4-2-2-2 and deservedly led.

The instigator was Oscar Bobb, sold by City in January, with a driving run on the right. Rodrigo Muniz’s first touch took him past Abdukodir Khusanov. His second was placed in the top corner. The striker celebrated by putting the ball up his shirt to mark his wife’s pregnancy. Muniz admitted he struggled last season when she had a miscarriage. It is too trite to say he looked a player reborn, but he gave Fulham a threat.

The opposing No 9 thought he had levelled. A disputed decision ensured otherwise, referee Thomas Bramall ruling Haaland had kicked the ball out of Bernd Leno’s hands when he bundled it over the line. “I had the ball in my hands,” the goalkeeper said. “I had the feeling I controlled the ball and Haaland crashed into me and slid into me.” City disagreed. “From my point of view it is quite clear that it is not a foul,” said Maresca. He said Haaland concurred, but the City top scorer may wish he had met Iliman Ndiaye’s cross with a better finish at the first time of asking.

It was not the only example of wastefulness. Haaland blazed over when released by Foden. Only three of City’s 15 shots were on target. They could have lost it. After recent errors, there was a redemptive element to Gianluigi Donnarumma’s saves from Bobb and Muniz. City’s winless streak nevertheless continued. “We don’t like this kind of moments in terms of four games in a row,” said Maresca. For Anderson, though, a different game brought a different status, as scorer and saviour.

Manchester City have been dealt a multi-billion-pound blow, following their guilty verdict over breaching Premier League rules.

In September, an independent panel ruled that Man City were guilty of over 100 charges of breaking financial rules, with the Premier League confirming the verdict in an official statement.

Richard Masters, Chief Executive of the Premier League, described the case as “the most significant in Premier League history”, with the league's own statement using the word “sham” five times.

While the Sky Blues face uncertainty on the pitch – including whether or not they will be relegated from the Premier League as a result of a points deduction – there has reportedly been an impact behind the scenes, too.

The Financial Times reports that United States-based investment firm Apollo Global Management have abandoned a $2 billion loan to City owner Sheikh Mansour – worth just over £1.5bn – following the Premier League's verdict.

Talks were ongoing over the arrangement between The City Football Group and the private capital group, who manage more than $1 trillion of assets and have already dealt with the likes of Atletico Madrid and Nottingham Forest previously.

According to the report, “The loan from Apollo would have provided the group, which also owns clubs in Europe, the Americas and Asia, with extra liquidity as well as being used to refinance existing credit facilities, according to people familiar with the matter.”

#1034. Could the AI boom make borrowing more expensive in Europe?

France, Germany and Italy face a volatile bond market as war inflation bites. With US tech giants now issuing billions in AI bonds, they are competing with cash-strapped European governments.

With more than $1 trillion (€900 billion) pouring into the artificial intelligence (AI) buildout, US tech giants are now competing with governments and companies in Europe for the same investment capital.

Four of the Big Five hyperscalers — Amazon, Google owner Alphabet, Meta and Oracle — have issued about $250 billion in bonds in dollars since the beginning of 2025, according to a tally of filings to US financial regulators by AI Industry Reviews, an independent platform that evaluates AI tools. They have sold a further €37 billion ($41 billion) of bonds in euros.

Recently, Microsoft, the last of the Big Five to hold back, joined the AI borrowing spree with a $25 billion bond sale, all in dollars.

Next year, Goldman Sachs projects that total new AI hyperscaler bond sales are expected to reach $420 billion. About €60 billion will be issued in euros, according to Dutch bank ING.

That is unwelcome news for European companies and countries like France, Germany and Italy, whose sovereign bond yields have risen sharply in recent months and are already straining public finances.

With public debt at 119% of gross domestic product (GDP) and a deficit still running above 5%, France is already paying a sizable risk premium on its debt. Over the past six months, yields on French 10-year bonds have climbed from roughly 3.7% to nearly 5%.

The French government's interest bill is set to rise from €79 billion currently to €91 billion next year and over €100 billion by 2028.

Based on these figures alone, France's Finance Ministry needs to find tens of billions of euros in additional cuts, tax hikes, or more borrowing by the end of the decade.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In August, economists at the European Central Bank said the euro bond market was adapting well to the presence of AI giants but warned they "could make it harder for other companies and other economic sectors to access finance."

Writing in a blog post, they also questioned whether the bloc's financial markets can "smoothly handle such large and concentrated debt inflows and warned of a "potential spillover to the sovereign and supranational segment of the bond market."

That means governments and international lenders such as the European Union and the European Investment Bank could also end up paying more to borrow.

Viktor Hjort, global head of credit strategy at the French bank BNP Paribas, described the phenomenon as "bond abundance."

Hjort told DW that the presence of the hyperscalers in the euro bond market is "already high enough to create competition" within the corporate sector and "between corporates and governments for available fixed income funds." These are investment funds that mostly buy bonds, which pay regular interest.

Bond yields jumped again last month, driven by rebounding energy prices linked to the Iran war and France’s political crisis, which Hjort said further revealed the growing competition for capital, as government and company borrowing costs rose together.

Normally, nervous investors move into government bonds during uncertain times, which pushes their borrowing costs down.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Goldman Sachs warned last week that rising interest costs were starting to hurt earnings at European companies. Among firms in the Stoxx 600 — an index of 600 large, mid-sized and small companies across Europe — Goldman found that interest costs as a share of sales have risen by nearly half since 2022.

The bank's analysts said this had cut earnings by more than 5% over the same period.

Factor in the competition from AI bonds, and European firms could now face pressure to cut their investments in new plants, equipment and research, as well as shareholder payouts, to prioritize loan repayments.

The pressure doesn't stop at national governments. Europe's cities and regions, whose borrowing helps to fund schools, transport and infrastructure, may also feel the effects of the AI boom.

A study for the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development(OECD), published in January, compared local bond markets in Belgium, Germany, Spain, Sweden and Canada. Where AI was spreading fastest, measured by the share of AI-related job vacancies, borrowing costs for cities and regions tended to rise.

"Whereas in the United States, my research has found that AI investments are linked to a lower cost of borrowing for municipalities, the opposite appears to hold in several European countries," the study's co-author, Christos Makridis of Arizona State University's W. P. Carey School of Business, told DW.

While AI bonds are far from the sole cause of Europe's widening fiscal strains, US Big Tech's huge appetite for capital could add further pressure next year, due to the additional billions in new bonds planned.

The irony is that European taxpayers could end up paying more on their own governments' debt, partly to help finance an AI boom across the Atlantic.

#1033. Thomas Frank’s Crystal Palace bow ends in own-goal heartbreak

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Coventry 3-2 Crystal Palace: The Eagles had twice come from behind to level at Coventry before Dwight McNeil’s own goal

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Thomas Frank suffered defeat in his first game as Crystal Palace boss as Dwight McNeil’s late own goal condemned them to a 3-2 loss at Coventry.

Frank, who was sacked by Tottenham in February, oversaw his first game for a third London club but was unable to stop them from losing for a fifth successive match in the Premier League.

Frank’s tenure got off to the worst start possible when Taiwo Awoniyi put the hosts in front with his second goal of the campaign, but Palace instantly responded through Yeremy Pino.

An all-action first half continued as Tatsuhiro Sakamoto’s sublime strike put Coventry back in front before Jorgen Strand Larsen’s first goal since September pulled Palace level again.

It looked like Palace would come away with a point until McNeil inadvertently bundled the ball into his own net to secure Coventry back-to-back home wins.

Frank Lampard’s side are growing in confidence in front of their own supporters and picked up a third win at the Coventry Building Society Arena.

Lampard was wary of the visitors starting strongly with a new boss, but it was his side who drew first blood when Jack Rudoni played the ball across for Awoniyi to stab a first-time effort into the far corner.

The hosts were left wondering how they were not two to the good when, seconds after Carl Rushworth’s save down one end, the Sky Blues broke through Awoniyi and he rounded Dean Henderson but saw his effort blocked heroically by Axel Disasi on the goal-line.

They were made to pay shortly afterwards as Palace levelled.

Daichi Kamada sent a cross in towards Strand Larsen who saw his failed scorpion attempt bounce kindly for Pino and he lashed home from close range.

Coventry regained their advantage on the half-hour mark courtesy of a sublime hit by Sakamoto.

Rudoni had assisted the first and was the creator again as he whipped a cross to Sakamoto who took a lovely touch with his chest before lashing a shot past Henderson from outside the box.

Palace came from behind for a second time on the stroke of half-time. Pino turned creator with a cross onto the head of Strand Larsen, who had sprung the offside the trap and nodded the ball beyond Rushworth.

Henderson was called into action to stop Coventry from going ahead for a third time as he dived to his right to palm Rudoni’s effort behind.

Palace were in the ascendancy and looking most likely to get their noses in front.

Strand Larsen was first onto a low cross by Pino but he was stopped by Rushworth and Bobby Thomas made a crucial block to stop substitute Evann Guessand from sweeping the ball home.

It proved vital as Coventry snatched a winner. Brandon Thomas-Asante’s initial header was saved by Henderson but the ball bounced off McNeil and rolled over the line.

#1032. Frick enjoys winning start with Aberdeen with victory at Kilmarnock

Kilmarnock vs Aberdeen. Scottish Premiership.

Report as Mario Frick makes a winning start as Aberdeen head coach; Kevin Nisbet scored a double in their 4-2 win at Kilmarnock; the Dons are up to eighth in the Scottish Premiership; Killie remain bottom

Mario Frick enjoyed a dream start to life as Aberdeen boss by edging a six-goal thriller with a 4-2 win over Kilmarnock.

Kevin Nisbet's double, coupled with Brad Lyons and Findlay Marshall strikes, secured three priceless Scottish Premiership points to leave the Rugby Park side rooted to the bottom.

The visitors climbed to eighth spot after a remarkable afternoon where they hit a much-needed scoring streak.

The Dons opted to dispense with the services of boss Stephen Robinson after a run of only one win from seven which saw them sink to second-bottom and Frick was appointed as his replacement last Sunday.

It should have been advantage to the hosts in the seventh minute as Greg Kiltie picked out Joe Hugill and the striker went one-on-one with Marius Muller but could only rattle his shot into the body of the Dons 'keeper. They were made to pay moments later.

Another slick Aberdeen attack had skipper Nisbet taking full advantage of some familiar hesitancy in the Killie defence to sidefoot a shot into Nico Mantl's bottom left-hand corner and Frick's reign was off and running in emphatic style.

It would get better in the 10th minute as Ieuan Owen was booked for a cynical foul on Nicky Devlin and Nisbet stepped up to brilliantly curl his 20-yard free-kick low past Mantl via post for his 15th goal of the season.

As the Red Army celebrated an astonishing reversal of fortunes, Hicham Mahou rattled a shot in from distance which sailed inches wide of the target as Killie struggled to regroup from the double-whammy but the pulled one back in the 20th minute.

It was a much-needed response as Greg Kiltie reacted first to a loose ball to drive a low shot past Muller and at a stroke the contest was back in the balance.

That would shift again on the half-hour mark as the Dons made it three with Lyons running onto a Nesta Guinness-Walker cross from the left to bury a header past Mantl as the goal-fest continued.

Killie almost reduced the deficit moments after the restart as Michael Schjonning-Larsen's strike was superbly turned away by Muller as the Rugby Park side looked to launch a rescue act.

Manti then blocked a Nisbet shot with his legs as the Scotland international went in search of his hat-trick in the 52nd minute but Kilie were still in the fight and they threw themselves a lifeline five minutes later as Muller gifted possession to Tyreece John-Jules who gratefully accepted by clipping his finish high into the net.

Jamie Brandon squandered a terrific chance to square the game in the 73rd when he blazed a shot over the bar from 16 yards with the goal gaping and with that the Dons held on to see out a contest which allows Frisk to get off to a winning start as the last word went to Marshall who drilled in a fourth three minutes from time.

Mario Frick predicted Kevin Nisbet would get his name on the scoresheet:

"I spoke to Kevin during the week and told him he would score and he scored twice, so he showed how dangerous he is inside the box. He could have scored three but I was very happy for him.

"I can enjoy it now but during the game it was difficult. We were lucky as well as Killie played very well, especially in the second half.

"We had some difficulties but in the end it was a deserved victory. We can defend better as we were lucky, We struggled in the first five or six minutes but after taking the lead we played well. But it was a bit chaotic and I was surprised.

"I told the players to play the way they did when they were young and they didn't think about mistakes or any negatives and played only to win for fun. I told them to play as they did as young players. Watching the third goal was beautiful, it's only the start and a beginning as we need to improve."

Killie boss Neil McCann admitted their winless run has to end, quickly:

"We are just conceding cheap goals and the boys are working so hard in training but when it comes into a game then that's when you really need to execute as that's when it matters most.

"When we managed to get ourselves back into the game at 2-1 I felt that we would go on and create more chances and then we conceded a third.

"In the second half we changed things around a bit as well as some personnel and adjusted how we were playing and I felt from the start of the second half onwards we were the better side.

"We were done on the counter-attack for the fourth goal and when you strip it all down I probably sound like a broken record. but the amount of chances we created and didn't take them....

"It's a sore one as we have worked so hard but it's in games where it matters most and every game is a chance to arrest that."

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Tottenham 2-0 Ipswich: Roberto De Zerbi turned to the 18-year-old after two bright cameos and the highly-rated Spurs attacker delivered with aplomb

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Luca Williams-Barnett lived up to the hype with a sparking display on his full debut for Tottenham to inspire a 2-0 win over Ipswich.

Roberto De Zerbi turned to the 18-year-old after two bright cameos and the highly-rated Spurs attacker delivered with aplomb, scoring on his first Premier League start after 15 minutes before a mazy run set up Dominic Solanke at the start of the second half.

After Williams-Barnett made his senior debut at the age of 16 last season, the clamour for the teenager to play has only increased during a difficult last 12 months and with injuries to Mathys Tel and Mykhailo Mudryk, the England Under-19 international grasped his chance to show why he has been hailed as a “special talent” by De Zerbi.

It was not a completely positive afternoon for De Zerbi with Savio forced off late on with a problem on his comeback after a seven-week lay-off.

However, this victory made it three home wins in a row for Tottenham in the Premier League for the first time in two years in further evidence a corner may have been turned in N17.

The excitement was palpable when it was confirmed Williams-Barnett would earn a first start for Tottenham with De Zerbi making six changes from the defeat at Leeds.

Gary O’Neil also shuffled his pack and went to a back five, but Ipswich started strongly and Antonin Kinsky was forced to deny Abdoul Ouattara and Zian Flemming in quick succession.

With De Zerbi in the stand due to a touchline ban, Spurs slowly started to get on top with Solanke curling wide before Williams-Barnett had the crowd on their feet with two dangerous crosses after lightning-quick step-overs.

Solanke went close again with a header across goal before Christian Walton denied the Tottenham forward from another set-piece, but the breakthrough arrived in 15th minute and via teenage sensation Williams-Barnett.

Pedro Porro was the architect with a wonderful cross from the right-hand side and Williams-Barnett showed excellent hunger to get ahead of Ouattara before he bundled in with his left knee.

It made Williams-Barnett the youngest Tottenham scorer in the Premier League since Gareth Bale in 2007.

Spurs almost made it 2-0 by the half hour mark but Mohammed Kudus curled a fine free-kick against a post.

Ipswich threatened again soon after; the busy Conor Gallagher blocking an effort by Exequiel Palacios before Kinsky claimed a corner and James Maddison received a booking for a pull back on Julio Enciso.

There was still time for Williams-Barnett to have a header saved and Walton thwarted a Maddison curler before the break.

With the game still in the balance, Spurs required a second goal and Williams-Barnett stepped up to make the difference again in the 52nd minute.

After Williams-Barnett picked up the ball inside his own half, the 18-year-old raced past Darnell Furlong and sent across an inch-perfect cross for Solanke to slide home his third goal this season.

Williams-Barnett accepted the acclaim before he left to a standing ovation with 26 minutes left.

After Walton prevented an own-goal by Ipswich captain Dara O’Shea, a minute’s applause in memory of Danny Kelly followed in the 69th minute and whilst Savio was forced off not long after his cross hit a post, Tottenham made it four wins in five.

#1029. Asian Cup postponed due to Middle East conflict

The Asian Cup has become the latest sporting event to be affected by the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. Organizers cite "exceptional circumstances" in Saudi Arabia, which has seen several Houthi attacks of late.

A little over two months before it was set to kick off, the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) has postponed its flagship international football tournament in the wake of recent deadly attacks on host country, Saudi Arabia.

The AFC cited "substantial logistical complexities and travel disruptions" caused by conflicts in the region.

Instead of January 7, 2027, the tournament will now kick off on December 23 and end on January 21, 2028. The postponement follows delays and cancellations of a number of sporting events in the region, including a Formula One race, the men's and women's tennis finals, the 2027 Dakar Rally and disruption to Asia's marquee continental club football tournament, the AFC Champions League Elite.

Saudi Arabia hosted, and won, the Gulf Cup last month, but there had already been much talk about whether the much larger Asian Cup could go ahead.

It was scheduled to feature 24 teams playing matches in eight venues across Riyadh, Jeddah and Khobar. However, the AFC said that "circumstances arising from developments in the region, including substantial logistical complexities and travel disruptions," made the tournament impossible.

"Exceptional circumstances have been created for the organization and delivery of the competition as originally scheduled, making the postponement necessary in the interest of all participating teams, officials, spectators and other stakeholders."

In particular, the postponement was forced by a recent wave of deadly attacks on Saudi Arabia by Iran-backed Houthi rebels as well as other raging conflicts in the region. The Houthis have targeted Saudi infrastructure, including airports. They are fighting a Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen's internationally recognized government, a civil war that reignited in July following a years-long truce.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The AFC had been under pressure from several federations to postpone the tournament, with South Korea's players leading the way.

"The ongoing military tensions and security instability in the Middle East are issues that cannot be taken lightly," Lee Keun-ho, president of the Korea Professional Footballers Association, said last month, according to the Yonhap News Agency.

Lee added that "no tournament's value can take precedence over the lives and safety of players and football fans."

It seems that the AFC now agrees. However, following the announcement of the postponement, Yasser al-Misehal, chairman of the local organizing committee, promised that Saudi Arabia was "fully ready" whenever the tournament ended up being held.

"The tournament will move to the new dates, and our preparations will continue as planned," he told the Saudi Press Agency.

"We're working closely with the AFC and all our partners to make sure the tournament runs smoothly and meets the high standards expected of Saudi Arabia and the Asian Cup."

Saudi Arabia has invested hugely in sports over the last decade, from owning Premier League teams to hosting boxing title fights and bidding for a number of major sporting events, most notably World Cup 2034, which they won the right to host unopposed.

However, the country has recently withdrawn or slashed funding for a number of sporting events including golf, rugby, tennis and winter sports.

Here is my verdict on the most popular names.

Jan Paul van Hecke (£5.1m): One of the best defenders to own. He is guaranteed to play, reliable for defensive contributions and a threat from set-pieces. Spurs' next three fixtures are Ipswich, Sunderland and Fulham, which is incredibly solid. Verdict: BUY

#1027. Bournemouth climb up to fourth after securing ninth victory in a row

Bournemouth 2-0 Nottingham Forest: Evanilson and Justin Kluivert were on target for the Cherries

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Bournemouth extended their winning run to nine in all competitions as Evanilson scored for the sixth Premier League game in a row in a 2-0 win over Nottingham Forest.

Justin Kluivert was also on target to help Marco Rose’s Cherries climb up to the dizzying heights of fourth place in the table.

The defeat means Forest are only above the relegation places on goal difference having failed to build on the momentum of their 3-1 win over Manchester City before the international break.

Both teams started the game on the front foot and Forest had the first sight of goal. Neco Williams nodded dangerously across the face of goal at the far post, but Liam Delap was beaten to the ball by home defender Antonio Silva.

Evanilson was denied by a brilliant last-ditch tackle from Forest centre-back Jair Cunha before Marcus Tavernier’s 20-yard curler was well saved by Matz Sels.

Bournemouth took the lead through Evanilson in the 19th minute. James Hill cushioned a header into the path of Evanilson, and the in-form Brazilian took one touch before blasting a left-footed shot into the roof of the net.

Kluivert almost doubled the home side’s lead with an effort from the edge of the penalty area which sailed narrowly over the crossbar.

Evanilson then failed to keep his shot down after a long throw from Hill caused chaos in the Forest penalty area.

Oliver Glasner’s side had a penalty appeal waved away when Adam Smith blocked Williams’s effort into the arm of team-mate Tyler Adams.

Kluivert did make it 2-0 on the stroke of half-time with a simple far-post finish after a superb run and cross from Tavernier.

Forest were much improved in the second half, adopting a more direct approach in a bid to forage a way back into the game.

Delap turned provider by whipping in a cross for captain Morgan Gibbs-White but the England international could not properly connect with his header.

James McAtee ballooned an effort over the crossbar as the visitors continued to misfire in front of goal.

Substitute Chris Wood also miscued a header from a corner when he should have at least tested underworked Bournemouth goalkeeper Dorde Petrovic.

Bournemouth always looked a threat on the counter and Kluivert came close to his second and the Cherries’ third when he stung the gloves of Selz from 18 yards out.

Kluivert should also have been more clinical when he found himself within finishing range but unselfishly laid the ball off to Rayan and the chance went begging.

Aston Villa 0-0 Sunderland: Unai Emery’s team had the better of a game of few chances

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Aston Villa and Sunderland drew a blank in their Premier League match at Villa Park.

Unai Emery’s team had the better of a game of few chances but failed to make the breakthrough and are now without a win in five games in all competitions.

Sunderland, bidding to move away from the relegation zone, ended a run of three successive away defeats with the 0-0 draw.

Aaron Wan-Bissaka and Emiliano Buendia returned for Villa at the expense of Victor Lindelof and John McGinn, who was on the bench.

Sunderland also made two changes, with Jules Ahoka and Wilson Isidor replacing the injured Granit Xhaka and Brian Brobbey.

The home side were on the front foot from the off and forced a couple of early corners, which came to nothing.

They had to wait until the 19th minute for their first chance, with Johan Manzambi’s low effort saved by Robin Roefs.

The Sunderland goalkeeper had a let-off in the 40th minute when he gifted possession to Buendia but recovered to claim the Villa midfielder’s weak shot.

Ian Maatsen threatened to break the deadlock in the early stages of the second half, but he could only follow an impressive run with a shot straight at Roefs.

Soon after the Black Cats, who created little of note before half-time, forced their first corner but failed to produce anything worthwhile from it.

Villa’s Leon Goretzka was then booked for pulling back Chemsdine Talbi, but Enzo Le Fee’s free-kick evaded Nordi Mukiele and was collected by goalkeeper Zion Suzuki.

As Villa fans chanted for the introduction of McGinn, Le Fee fired narrowly wide.

The home faithful got what they wanted just before the hour mark when McGinn was introduced, alongside Ibrahim Mbaye.

The Scotland international had a chance to open the scoring midway through the second half but fired over.

Sunderland won a free-kick 25 yards out when Goretzka fouled Le Fee, but the midfielder’s effort was straight at Suzuki.

Villa boss Emery made another double substitution in the 73rd minute, with Brian Madjo and Ross Barkley replacing Nicolas Jackson and Goretzka.

The home side pressed for a winner and, after McGinn failed to find the target three minutes later, Barkley forced Roefs to tip over a powerful effort from distance.

Roefs reacted sharply to prevent Mukiele heading into his own goal, then Alysson fired over.

The visitors almost stole a win in the first of three added minutes, but Talbi’s curling right-foot effort went narrowly wide of Suzuki’s far post.

#1024. Football: Spanish player dies on after cardiac arrest on the pitch

Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel has died following a collision with the opposing goalkeeper. The Spanish second-division club has said it is "heartbroken" by the loss.

"Heartbroken with pain, with a lump in our throat and unable to believe this is real." Those were the words with which Spanish second division football club Tenerife confirmed the death of 30-year-old Jesus de Miguel on Tuesday.

De Miguel was involved in a clash in the middle of the pitch with FC Andorra's Equatorial Guinea international goalkeeper Jesus Owono, who had raced out of his goal to try and clear the ball with the score 2-2 late in the game. Owono was sent off and the match was abandoned.

Spanish media reported that De Miguel suffered a cardiac arrest and was resuscitated. The player was taken to hospital and placed in intensive care, with Tenerife later saying that De Miguel's condition had "worsened neurologically" before his death.

After confirming the death on Tuesday morning, the club posted that: "No words can ease the pain, nothing can lessen this great feeling of sadness. Our thoughts are with the family, his close friends and Tenerife fans, who today are grieving over this terrible news."

Andorra also sent their "most sincere condolences" as messages of support began to flood in on Tuesday.

"I am so deeply sorry. Rest in peace, Jesus," former Barcelona defender Gerard Pique, Andorra's majority shareholder, wrote on social media.

Real Madrid, Barcelona, Atletico Madrid and other clubs in Spain also sent messages of condolence, as well as the Spanish FA (RFEF).

"Shattered by this sad news, the Royal Spanish Football Federation wishes to express our deepest sorrow at his passing today," wrote the federation in a statement.

The RFEF postponed Tuesday's matches in the Copa del Rey and Copa de la Reina, "as a gesture of respect and solidarity."

De Miguel had been with Tenerife since joining from from Castellon in 2025. He began his career with Leganes at youth level in the Madrid suburbs, playing for a string of teams, including Unionistas de Salamanca, before signing for Castellon in 2023.

Edwin van der Sar has his wife to thank for quickly spotting the symptoms when he suffered a brain haemorrhage in 2023.

The former Ajax, Juventus, Fulham and Manchester United great has since gone on to make a full recovery, and appeared for an Ajax Legends side against their Barcelona counterparts at the Johan Cruyff Arena last weekend.

But at the time it happened, Van der Sar's wife, Annemarie van Kesteren, knew exactly what was happening having suffered a brain haemorrhage herself back in 2009.

Van der Sar told FourFourTwo: "Annemarie knew what was happening. I had this strange feeling that something wasn't right.

"Then before you know it, you see the light and the light hurts your eyes. I had pain in my head.

"From that point onwards, you just let yourself go, and hope the ambulance and the people around you take care of you.

"You have to put your faith, your life, into the hands of people who are trained for that and who specialise in it."

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

In a way, Van der Sar considers the timing to be fortuitous: he had only recent resigned as Ajax chief executive after seven years in the post.

He said: "I'd stepped away five or six weeks before [from Ajax], so I had all the time in the world to recover, rest and get better.

"If I'd still had the job, I think the eagerness and the demands of the position might have made my recovery harder.

"When you're responsible for a club, a company or an organisation, you want to be there.

"Luckily, I had no ties and nothing else to focus on apart from myself and my recovery. I've had a few chats - but nothing has really felt right.

"I'm enjoying my life at the moment, and I'm not actively looking for another position."

Chelsea will be sweating over the fitness of their midfield lynchpin after this latest setback

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Moises Caicedo was forced off in the first half of Chelsea’s thrashing by Leeds as Xabi Alonso’s injury problems continue to mount.

The Ecuadorian lynchpin suffered a bad landing after meeting James Justin’s aerial challenge, which saw him twist in midair and land on his tailbone.

Caicedo was initially able to continue but after being troubled by his back in the following minutes, repeatedly holding the problem area, he went down off the ball, covering his seemingly tearful eyes with his shirt in dejection.

He was replaced by Jordan Henderson in the 22nd minute, but did not go straight down the tunnel for further treatment, instead taking a seat on the bench with an ice pack.

Alonso said after the 4-1 defeat that Caicedo had picked up a “knock” and that Chelsea would have to wait and see following further assessments on Sunday.

“He was in pain and let's see how bad it is,” Alonso said.

The circumstances in which Caicedo’s injury was dealt with left the Chelsea dugout unhappy with referee Michael Oliver.

Caicedo agonised on the deck for a considerable period before the Blues eventually sent their medical team on to treat him, with club doctors delaying their entry onto the pitch to try and prevent him having to come off for a minute, as per a new rule introduced in the Premier League this season.

Seemingly for the same reason, Caicedo leapt up and refused treatment from Chelsea medics when they approached him, but Oliver still ordered him to the touchline, reducing Chelsea to 10 men for a minute.

Caicedo also suffered a fitness scare during the international break when he was replaced at half-time of Ecuador’s 2-0 friendly win over Bolivia in midweek after feeling unwell.

The Blues are already without a number of key members due to injury including Reece James, Maxence Lacroix and Joao Pedro, with the club struggling for form following four defeats in five.

#1021. Sore throat? The brain has surprising control over how ill you feel

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Max Kozlov is a senior reporter with Nature in Washington DC.

Researchers are beginning to show how neurons in the brain detect an infection and tailor physiological responses to fight it.Credit: Dr. Chris Henstridge/SPL

A viral cold or bacterial infection can leave you feeling miserable, but each infection produces its own mix of symptoms. Now, neuroscientists are discovering that the brain is the conductor of these responses — decoding the type of pathogen that has invaded, accessing memories of past bouts of illness and even mobilizing immune defences at the sight of a sick person.

The findings, many of which are unpublished, were presented on 15 November at the Society for Neuroscience annual meeting in Washington DC, and challenge the established view of what it means to feel unwell. Neuroscientists have long viewed neurological responses to infection as a one-size-fits-all response to inflammation, rather than a strategy tailored to the threat.

“Sickness is actually not a fixed program, although we often talk about it this way,” said Jessica Osterhout, a neurobiologist at the University of Utah in Salt Lake City, who chaired the session.

A bacterial infection and a cold caused by a virus can both result in fever and exhaustion, yet they rarely trigger the same constellation of symptoms. Bacterial infections, for instance, tend to suppress appetite much more sharply than do colds, which made Osterhout and her colleagues wonder how the brain tells various pathogens apart.

Your brain could be controlling how sick you get — and how you recover

Your brain could be controlling how sick you get — and how you recover

In unpublished experiments, Osterhout’s team compared mice injected with a bacterial toxin with those given a compound that mimics a viral infection. To see how the brain distinguished between pathogens, the researchers profiled individual cells in circumventricular organs, which are specialized structures with unusually permeable blood vessels that surround brain ventricles.

When the body has an infection, cells in the circumventricular organs switch on sets of immune-related genes and release distinct mixes of chemical signals. Those signals diffuse to nearby neurons and create distinct patterns of activity for different pathogens, allowing the brain to customize its symptom profile depending on the threat.

Rather than acting as conduits that let inflammatory signals pass unchecked from the blood into the wider brain, these structures “may actually interpret them”, Osterhout said.

Sometimes, the brain doesn’t even wait for pathogens to enter the body to rally the immune system1. Andrea Serino, a neuroscientist at Lausanne University Hospital in Switzerland, studies how the brain maps peripersonal space, which is the area around the body roughly in arm’s reach.

When Serino’s team placed volunteers in virtual reality, they found that threat-monitoring brain regions became active when avatars bearing skin lesions caused by viral or bacterial infections approached, even when the figures were beyond arm’s reach. Just 15 minutes of virtual exposure triggered a surge in frontline immune ‘sentinel’ cells in participants’ blood comparable to that induced by an influenza vaccine. This reaction did not occur when participants saw healthy-looking avatars or ones expressing fear.

These experiments suggest that the immune system uses “the predictive ability of the brain to react before pathogens enter the body”, Serino said.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03774-w

#1020. How Berlin's Arab queers are building their community

As the co-founder of the ADIRA Drag Festival, Lebanese performance artist, drag performer, DJ and cultural organizer Hassandra has become an essential part of Berlin's queer artistic landscape.

"Adira" is an Arabic slang term used in Levantine queer culture to describe someone with a strong presence — someone powerful and accomplished.

It is also the name of a Berlin-based collective that curates events and club nights celebrating the diversity of queer Arab* culture. The asterisk signals the inclusion of non-Arab ethnic minorities and people with diverse identities and roots in Southwest Asia and North Africa.

Among the collective's events is the ADIRA Drag Festival, which celebrated its third edition in Berlin in late October.

This year's theme, "Who's Your Diva?!," brought together drag performers paying tribute to legendary figures from across the Eastern Mediterranean who have become queer icons — from Egyptian music legend Umm Kulthum to Turkish star Bülent Ersoy and Lebanese pop icon Haifa Wehbe.

Hassandra, co-founder of ADIRA and the ADIRA Drag Festival, was among the performers, taking on the persona of Lebanese pop star Elissa.

"It is very important for me to bring my Lebanese Arab identity and culture into what I do, because I think it's a very beautiful culture. And there's a lot of campy, glamorous, beautiful divas," Hassandra said.

Elissa's "whole discography is very romantic, raw, soft, kind of like very Adele vibes," Hassandra told DW ahead of the October 30 show. "However, her personality is known to be the extreme opposite. She's very feisty. Very blunt, very unfiltered. Not soft at all as a person."

The star is also known for speaking out on political issues in Lebanon. She has publicly voiced support for LGBTQ+ communities in the Middle East, while also frequently sparking controversy across the Arab world with her outspoken positions on other political issues.

Hassandra's ADIRA Drag Festival performance addresses this complexity, ultimately "tapping into her sort of controversial political opinions," the drag artist explained.

This reflects one of the ideas Hassandra hopes to promote with the theme of this year's festival. "As queer people, we tend to idealize a lot of pop divas. But these pop divas are very imperfect in their nature," Hassandra said. The show provides an opportunity to critically revisit these divas' legacy through a more critical lens.

"And this sort of critical lens can be taken into the outside world, as in: never follow anyone in life blindly. No one should follow any politician, any political party, any pop diva, any activist blindly."

Born in Beirut in 1994, Hassandra studied theater and stage acting at the Lebanese University before moving to Berlin in 2017. "I would say it was it was just a very sort of impulsive decision at the age of 22. I mean, there's no doubt that the economic situation was really bad in Lebanon and continued to become even worse," the artist said.

In Berlin, Hassandra became increasingly involved in the city's independent art scene and queer nightlife. Drag emerged as another form of self-expression for the actor.

Through performances that combine theatrical intensity, political humor, grotesque aesthetics and moments of tenderness, Hassandra challenges conventional understandings of gender and identity.

Their work explores themes of home, nostalgia, displacement and queer Arab culture. These ideas are also central to ADIRA, which Hassandra founded in 2023 with Syrian-German DJ and cultural producer Zuher Jazmati, also known as xanax_attax.

Through panel discussions, performances and music events, ADIRA fosters collective participation and community-building.

As Islamophobia and homophobia rise alongside the far right, spaces like ADIRA offer a sense of belonging and support for Arab queer communities.

That sense of community has become even more important following the deadly Islamist terrorist attack during Berlin's Christopher Street Day pride parade in July.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In the aftermath, Hassandra felt caught between their different identities. As an Arab queer person, "you fall in this position where then you start receiving a lot of racism," they said.

"And I think this is why it's important, for us queer Arabs, to say we are sad over what happened, but that we also reject any of the racism that comes from that," Hassandra said. "I think we [the Arab community] are being used in a lot of ways as a punching bag for a lot of things that are happening."

Rather than allowing the attack to fuel hatred and racism, Hassandra said, "we should make Germany a safer place for everyone to live in."  "There's place for everyone. It's a huge country," they added.

The interview with Hassandra was conducted by Gönna Ketels.

Chema Andres is quickly making Brighton fans forget about Carlos Baleba

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If there’s one thing Brighton and Hove Albion know how to do, it’s sell players for sizeable fees and replace them with bargain signings who prove to be just as good, if not better.

They replaced Yves Bissouma with Moises Caicedo, Robert Sanchez with Bart Verbruggen, Leandro Trossard with Kaoru Mitoma, and Marc Cucurella with Pervis Estupinan. Even when Caicedo and Alexis Mac Allister departed in the same summer, Brighton managed to maintain their upward trajectory thanks in part to the emergence of Carlos Baleba.

Now, having sold Baleba to Manchester United for £70 million, the Seagulls appear to have pulled off the same trick with another promising young midfielder: Chema Andres, who has developed a formidable partnership with veteran Pascal Gross in midfield.

Andres was still developing in Real Madrid’s academy less than two years ago. After honing his skills in the Spanish capital, he joined Stuttgart in 2025 for €3 million, where he quickly established himself as an important figure in midfield, steering them to a DFB-Pokal final and Champions League qualification.

He appeared destined to continue his development in Germany, but Brighton had other ideas. With just hours left in the summer transfer window, the Seagulls swooped in and signed him for £16 million. Fabian Hurzeler thrust him in at the deep end, and Andres quickly repaid his trust by assisting on his debut at Coventry and leading Brighton to an EFL Cup victory at Old Trafford.

A midfield masterclass from @BHAFC's Chema Andres 👏 https://t.co/9s4FUF7Kd2October 3, 2026

In just his second season of senior football, Andres is emerging as one of the Premier League’s top midfielders. Brighton sit second in the table, five points behind Arsenal, one ahead of Manchester City and 14 clear of relegation-threatened Manchester United. At the heart of their start is Andres, whose defensive discipline and penetrative passing has made him indispensable after Baleba's departure.

While Baleba’s greatest strength lies in his ball-carrying ability, Andres offers Brighton a different route through opposition defenses. According to Gradient Sports, a football analysis company, Andres is averaging 4.41 midfield line-breaking passes per 90 minutes, compared with Baleba’s 2.74 during his final season at Brighton. He is also completing 79.2% of these passes, well above Baleba’s 70.9%.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

That superiority extends to more audacious, high-risk passes: Andres is attempting 2.02 attacking line-breaking passes per 90, nearly twice Baleba’s 1.05, while completing them with far greater accuracy (90.9% vs. 71.4%). Whereas Baleba relied on his explosive acceleration to bypass opponents, Andres is using his vision, composure and passing range to slice through defensive lines and find his teammates.

Andres is also making his presence felt off the ball. While he might not be the same all-action midfielder who thrives on charging around the pitch and throwing himself into duels, his positional awareness and anticipation have proved invaluable in shielding Brighton’s backline. No Premier League midfielder has registered more tackles per 90 (3.31) or blocks per 90 (2.94) than Andres this season, while his 64.7% success rate in 50/50 duels exceeds Baleba’s 62.5%.

At 21 years-old, Andres is already imposing himself against the Premier League’s top sides. He excelled against Bruno Guimaraes and Declan Rice and found the back of the net in a 3–0 victory against defending champions Arsenal, before holding his own in a 1-0 win against Manchester City.

Despite costing Brighton less than a tenth of what City spent on Ayyoub Bouaddi, Elliot Anderson and Enzo Fernandez combined, Andrés helped the Seagulls secure their first away victory against City in 18 attempts, before playing a pivotal role in their hard-fought 2–0 win against Brentford.

For all his virtues, it would be premature to declare Andrés an outright upgrade on Baleba. Nevertheless, his passing intelligence, defensive anticipation and tactical discipline could make him an even better fit for Hurzeler’s system. Rather than simply replacing Baleba’s qualities, Brighton have found a midfielder whose strengths complement their style of play, once again demonstrating their knack for staying one step ahead of the transfer market.

For a club that has built its reputation on unearthing hidden gems, molding them into stars, and selling them for astronomical profits, Andres is shaping up to be another transfer masterstroke. And if he can help Brighton secure a maiden Champions League qualification, Baleba’s departure might be remembered not as a setback, but as the catalyst for the greatest moment in the club’s history.

After getting his big breakthrough as the co-founder of the football analytics website Breaking The Lines, Zachary Lowy has been able to tap into his footballing expertise for a number of esteemed outlets like ESPN, FotMob, The Times, The Independent and Urban Pitch. Since joining FourFourTwo as a freelancer in 2025, Lowy has been able to cover a wide range of topics from analyzing the sweeping changes to the MLS season to interviewing key figures like Asamoah Gyan and Rob Holding. Fluent in Spanish, Portuguese and Italian, Lowy’s versatile skillset has allowed him to traverse a number of different fields when covering major competitions like the FIFA Club World Cup. In addition to football, he is also a seasoned participant of other sports like pickleball, tennis, and volleyball.

Chelsea missed the chance to open up a four-point gap at the top of the Women’s Super League having been held to a goalless draw by Liverpool.

Sonia Bompastor’s side remain unbeaten this season but their advantage over Manchester City, who play Sunday, is only two points after failing to find a way past Khiara Keating in St Helens.

The Liverpool goalkeeper tipped over Alyssa Thompson’s shot and also denied Sandy Baltimore at full stretch in the first half, before keeping out Wieke Kaptein, Keira Walsh and Sjoeke Nusken in the second.

Liverpool had ended a five-match run without a win with victory at Brighton last weekend and they carried that confidence into the game against the league leaders to move up to eighth.

"I am really pleased,” Liverpool manager Gareth Taylor said. “The girls stuck to the game plan phenomenally well against a tough opponent and I cannot give them enough credit for what they did today. A lot of top individual performances and as a collective we really stuck to the task.

"They had some chances, we had some chances - ours were probably better. And then in the second half, we didn't have the same amount because it's fatiguing to replicate that pressure and at times we didn't keep the ball well enough.

“But credit to the players. I am so pleased they held on as sometimes you need that just for all your work.”

In the late kick-off, Danielle van de Donk and Alexia Putellas both scored twice as London City Lionesses closed the gap on Chelsea with a 6-2 victory against Crystal Palace.

Alanna Kennedy and Isobel Goodwin also found the net to draw Eder Maestre’s side to within four points of the leaders.

The Soccer Saturday legend on his remarkable 2026 journey from Borneo, and the most disastrous choice he could have made for a travel partner...

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Jeff Stelling hosted Soccer Saturday for 29 years between 1994 and 2023 – but the end of his tenure has given him the opportunity to explore the world this year.

Stelling is currently starring in BBC One show Celebrity Race Across The World, having recently travelled from Borneo to Malaysia alongside his son Matt.

The rules of the expedition, however, meant Stelling wasn’t allowed to contact home or find out the scores of his beloved Hartlepool United.

Among the competition in the other three pairs were singers Sam Ryder and Ella Eyre, plus the offspring of Katie Price and Peter Andre, although Stelling admits to FourFourTwo that the show wasn’t exactly relaxed.

“It was incredibly stressful, because you’ve got no phone, you can’t find the football scores – no credit cards, £26 a day between the two of you for transport, food and accommodation, and you find yourself sleeping on floors, surrounded by rats in some cases,” he told us.

“But you see the most incredible sights, things I didn’t know existed. It was an amazing experience.”

Even in the remote north of Australia, Stelling still heard the familiar catchphrase of 'Unbelievable, Jeff!' – once coined by his Soccer Saturday pal Chris Kamara.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“Wherever I go, someone will shout it and laugh as if it’s the first time it’s ever been done…” Stelling smiles – in this week’s episode, it was clear that hearing the catchphrase cheered him up, after a tough few days of travelling.

“It became part of football terminology – could you believe from the beginnings of Soccer Saturday that, 30 years later, people still use it? When I was in Australia, a gang of guys outside a hostel shouted it.”

Stelling travelled with his son on this occasion, having previously ventured to far-flung places with Kamara – heading to Sri Lanka on World’s Most Dangerous Roads.

If he’d had to choose a former footballer to travel with for Celebrity Race Across The World, who would have been the worst person he could have chosen?

“Oh, Gabby Agbonlahor,” Stelling replies instantly with a laugh, referencing his talkSPORT colleague. “His geographical knowledge isn’t quite of the standard required. He couldn’t do Race Across Birmingham!”

Stelling was speaking to FFT at the home of Woking FC as part of National League’s title sponsor Enterprise’s Local Legends campaign.

Nominations are being invited for unsung heroes across the league’s three divisions, with six eventually chosen to have their faces displayed on Wembley Way on National League play-off final weekend in May. Enterprise will also donate to community or charitable initiatives of all six associated clubs.

“In the National League, and National League North and South, virtually every club is the heartbeat of the community – there’s no other occasion when so many people from different walks of life within that community will be together,” says Stelling, whose boyhood club returned to the National League in 2023.

“Watching Hartlepool isn’t always therapeutic, but there’s nothing bigger in the community than Hartlepool United.

“For clubs like us, when the good times are so few and far between, you remember them far better. When we won promotion from the National League to the Football League in 2021, it was one of the greatest days of my life.”

There will be more from Stelling on his career in football in the next issue of FourFourTwo magazine.

Jeff Stelling has launched Enterprise’s search for the National League’s Local Legends – celebrating those who turn up for their club and community week in, week out. Click here to nominate.

#1016. Chelsea’s deep and ongoing issues revealed by Leeds drubbing

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Chelsea 1-4 Leeds United: As the Blues drop to eighth in the table, Xabi Alonso must do more to address the lack of culture at the club

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

By the end, amid what Xabi Alonso described as a “fragile moment”, even his own cultured touch had deserted him. As his Chelsea team tried to offer something in the final minutes of an utterly nothing performance against a brilliant Leeds United, the ball was easily cleared for a throw. Alonso, famed for his technique as a player, miscontrolled it towards his underwhelming bench.

He’s now seeing his reputation as a coach plummet, as Chelsea fall to eighth. This 4-1 evisceration was not just Leeds’ first win at the home of their old Seventies rivals since 1999 – to add to how Tottenham Hotspur also won here a few weeks ago – but a second defeat in a row, and a fifth in 11 this season.

And yet the very nature of it was still worse than any numbers can tell.

Outside an early Emmanuel Emegha goal on his first start, there was nothing to speak positively about, and just nothing about Chelsea.

Leeds found it easy to get at them, and they were soon rampaging through them.

They could have been 3-1 up by half-time, after Noah Okafor’s well-taken equaliser, but it never looked like it would take long to get there in the second half.

And, sure, Chelsea might well dispute the absurd-looking handball decision that eventually gave Dominic Calvert-Lewin his goal to make it 2-1, but they couldn’t dispute that it was coming.

Leeds were rampant, Okafor soon lashing in his second from yet another poorly-defended set-piece. There, Austin MacPhee’s influence becomes just one more aspect to question about the first team.

The manner of Brenden Aaronson’s goal, as he was allowed to just surge through the team, summed the afternoon up.

Chelsea didn’t look a team. Leeds, by contrast, knew exactly what they were about in every moment of the game. They had an identity.

Chelsea are instead looking to individuals.

They lost all cohesion once Moises Caicedo again went off injured, having already lacked any bite without Joao Pedro.

The striker was nevertheless involved in what might actually have been one of the match’s most telling moments.

As Cole Palmer went off, Chelsea coach Willie Isa seemed to gesture the forward towards the fans.

There were admittedly very few left, and many of those had loudly booed on the final whistle. Palmer didn’t go over, and then seemed to have a few words with Joao Pedro, too.

“We were disappointed,” Alonso said afterwards.

Either way, there is probably a bigger point there, that emphasises how all this is bigger than the manager.

Yes, a coach as accomplished as Alonso should be doing better than this. There has been constant talk that some of the players haven’t found him as tactically sophisticated as they expected, something which has arguably manifested in how they seem to have got worse the more time he’s had with them – in the same way they got worse the longer this game went on.

To apparently have such little fight, and lose the club’s two biggest grudge matches at home for the first time in 67 years, is awful to have on your CV.

The kind of fight that can preserve that kind of record, however, comes from something deeper. It comes from culture.

It’s why there’s almost a symbolism in Isa having that word with Palmer after the game, given that the coach is seen as a “cultural architect”. One of his qualities is building the right mood at a club.

But how do you really do that when everything is changing all the time?

So, yes, Chelsea could reasonably ask questions of the manager. Fans already sound like they might want him out.

But it’s still just 11 games, in a situation where there has been constant upheaval.

Only eight regular Chelsea squad members have been there for three years or more. The longest-serving after the home-grown Reece James – again out today – and Levi Colwell is Wesley Fofana.

He’s been here since 2022, but has also been injured so often, to the point it’s hard not to wonder whether it’s prevented him reaching the performance level he is capable of.

And all of that as other signings have constantly swirled around them.

Yes, Chelsea may have recently made moves to address this, as illustrated with the signings of Jordan Henderson and Danny Welbeck.

You can’t just buy in culture, though. It isn’t plug in and play. It has to be developed over a long period, with, yes, individuals setting standards.

One or two players can’t do that on their own. There has to be something more.

There has to be something that a head coach can fit into, that he can amplify. Of course, Alonso has been named as a manager rather than head coach, because the job is so much bigger.

No wonder Chelsea are “fragile”, or struggling to recover when they “receive a punch”, as Alonso put it.

You withstand that through resilience, which comes from culture, which comes from principles.

Chelsea haven’t had any of that applied, really, since Thomas Tuchel. No coach has had enough time, either in the job or with a defined core of players.

The ebullient Daniel Farke, by contrast, knows his squad inside out. He was able to laugh about how the music they were playing – pumping through the away dressing-room wall – is a bit too loud for him.

His team ensured the visiting fans made plenty of noise. They knew exactly what they were about, because they know exactly what they are. They have an identity.

They closed Chelsea out when needed, and boxed them in when they wanted. It made the final score… inevitable. And yet, it could have been worse.

Alonso needs more than coaching to make this get better.

Arsenal are moving for a potential superstar, as they welcome a wonderkid to North London

Arsenal are causing a “transfer frenzy” in South America, over a highly-rated wonderkid.

That's according to a new report that says that the Premier League champions are looking to improve their squad over the long term, as much as they are interested in adding players who can help the team fight on three fronts.

FourFourTwo understands that manager Mikel Arteta is keen to add dynamic difference makers in attack – but Arsenal could well surprise everyone by adding a 19-year-old who isn't well-known to Premier League fans.

During Arteta's early tenure as manager, the Gunners leant into the South American market, bringing in Pablo Mari from Flamengo as the Basque boss's first signing, six months after landing Gabriel Martinelli from the fourth tier of Brazilian football.

Since then, Arteta has built around the likes of Gabriel Jesus and Gabriel Magalhaes, while bringing in Argentine assistant Gabriel Heinze.

The champions may be about to land their first Paraguayan, too, with Sport Witness relaying reports that teenage sensation Eduardo Delmas could be on his way to London.

According to information from Deporte Total, Arsenal are “seriously pursuing” Delmas, with Gunners scouts watching the attacker score in Paraguay's Superclasico and legendary forward Roque Santa Cruz providing his opinion on the starlet.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Delmas's club, Olimpia, meanwhile, are looking for a record sale for their talent, with the likes of Real Madrid and Paris Saint-Germain also scouting the talent.

Arteta may well be able to offer a pathway to the first team that the other two can't, however, with the likes of Max Dowman and Marli Salmon both making regular senior appearances for the Gunners after emerging recently from the famed Hale End academy.

During Arteta's time in charge, the likes of Bukayo Saka, Emile Smith Rowe and Eddie Nketiah have all played prominent roles, while Ethan Nwaneri, Folarin Balogun and Myles Lewis-Skelly have all been given Premier League debuts before the age of 21, to demonstrate Arsenal's commitment to developing youngsters.

The report suggests that “Olimpia will include numerous performance bonuses so that the operation could be worth even more than his current release clause,” though the initial fee will be a significant one, too.

Club president Rodrigo Nogues explained in September that he wanted Delmas to become Paraguayan football's biggest-ever sale, with an asking price set at over £10 million.

Arsenal travel to Newcastle United when Premier League action resumes this weekend.

#1014. From rotten food to political opponents: Researchers explore how disgust relates to our beliefs, and why the connection is complicated

Some studies have linked disgust sensitivity to socially conservative attitudes. But does disgust shape our politics, or do our beliefs shape what we find disgusting?

Some studies have linked disgust sensitivity to socially conservative attitudes.

But as Americans vote in the US midterm elections, it's time to think about how disgust shapes our politics, or whether our beliefs shape what we find disgusting?

The smell of rotten food can make us recoil. Certain sexual practices can provoke a similar reaction. And in today's polarized political climate, even political opponents can become objects of disgust.

Psychologists have long investigated whether sensitivity to disgust helps explain political beliefs. A review of 24 studies found that people who reported being more easily disgusted tended to hold more socially conservative views.

"We think that it evolved in part to reduce exposure to things that could make you sick," psychologist Yoel Inbar, of the University of British Columbia in Canada, told DW.

But disgust is not a single emotion. The Three-Domain Disgust Scale, developed in 2009, distinguishes three types:

One theory is that people who are especially wary of germs and disease may also prefer traditional social rules.

Inbar explains that avoiding potential sources of infection can also mean missing out on new experiences.

"Some people are more on the cautious conservative side, and some people are more on the exploring risk-taking side when it comes to pathogen exposure," he said.

Indeed, the language of contamination also appears in political rhetoric. During his 2024 presidential campaign, Donald Trump repeatedly described immigrants as "poisoning the blood of our country." Trump has also described himself as a "germaphobe."

Inbar acknowledges that the evidence linking sensitivity to disgust with conservative political beliefs remains uncertain.

"We have hypotheses. I don't know that we have as strong of evidence as I would like," Inbar said.

Disgust is not exclusively conservative. And what people find revolting can depend on their values.

A 2020 study titled "Is Disgust a "Conservative" Emotion?" found that liberals and conservatives were disgusted by different things.

Conservatives, generally aligned with the Republicans in US politics, reported greater disgust at examples involving sexual behaviors and drug use, while liberals, generally aligned with the Democrats, reported greater disgust at animal abuse and environmental pollution.

However, when asked how easily disgusted they were in general, there was no clear difference across the political spectrum.

Some early studies suggested conservatives showed stronger physical reactions to frightening or disgusting images, measured partly through changes in sweating.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But subsequent research, including a 2020 study by political psychologist Bert Bakker at the University of Amsterdam, struggled to reproduce those findings.

Studies based on questionnaires, however, have generally found that people with more conservative attitudes report being more easily disgusted.

"If bodily reactions don't differ across political groups, why do feelings?" Manos Tsakiris, of Royal Holloway and the Centre for the Politics of Feelings at the University of London, told DW.

Tsakiris and colleague Mariana von Mohr wondered whether the answer might lie in how people perceive and interpret signals from their bodies.

Scientists call the perception of internal sensations, such as hunger, breathing or a racing heart, "interoception." It's sometimes called our eighth sense, alongside the familiar five, plus our senses of balance and body position.

"A bodily signal doesn't arrive with a label attached," Tsakiris told DW. "We have to notice it and make sense of it."

The researchers surveyed 632 US adults, asking how much they noticed and trusted signals from their bodies — a measure known as "interoceptive sensibility."

They found that people who were more easily disgusted by sexual behavior tended to be more conservative, regardless of how aware they felt of their bodies.

But for moral disgust, the link to conservatism was found only among people who reported lower bodily awareness.

What particularly surprised Tsakiris was that perceived bodily awareness alone had no link to political views.

"People who are highly attuned to their bodies were neither more liberal nor more conservative," he said.

Inbar questions whether all forms of disgust are equally useful for studying political attitudes.

He and Joshua Tybur, one of the creators of the Three-Domain Disgust Scale, generally prefer measuring pathogen disgust — reactions to potential sources of disease — rather than sexual disgust.

Questions about sexual disgust may already reflect conservative beliefs about sex.

"It's almost asking people the same thing twice," Inbar said.

The new study found no significant link between pathogen disgust and conservative views.

Inbar wants the findings on bodily awareness and disgust tested again, with predictions set out in advance. For now, he considers them "suggestive at best."

Tsakiris suggests that people who struggle to understand their bodily feelings may be more vulnerable to political messages telling them what those feelings mean.

"I know what you're feeling. You're feeling angry or you're feeling disgusted about this thing," he said, illustrating how someone might put an emotional label on another person's unease.

Such labels could influence political behavior, he argues, although the study did not directly test this.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"This is how disgust can do political work: it can turn moral judgments about individuals into judgments about whole groups," he said.

The research cannot establish whether disgust shapes political beliefs or existing beliefs shape what people find disgusting. Bakker notes that political beliefs can influence how people describe their own personalities, suggesting the relationship could work both ways.

"Voting behavior is very complex and citizens make up their mind about politics in a complex way," he told DW.

Inbar also cautions against exaggerating disgust's importance. "The thing to emphasize in your story is that the relationship, while it's consistent, is quite small," he said.

"It's one of the many influences on people's politics."

Tsakiris advocates what he calls "critical feeling": questioning our emotional responses to provocative material, including social media posts, just as we question the information itself.

He also emphasizes discussing our feelings with others and listening to different perspectives, even when we disagree.

"Life and politics and democracy is a contact sport," he said. Edited by: Rosalie Delaney
