#897. How to turn impostor syndrome into a superpower

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Gemma Conroy is a freelance journalist in Mexico City and editor of Nature Briefing: Careers.

Impostor syndrome — a fear of being less competent than people think — is common in researchers. Credit: Gandee Vasan/Getty

In 2021, Kwabena Boahen Asare found himself in at the deep end when he joined a skin cancer laboratory to gain hands-on research experience.

For Asare, who was a first-year undergraduate student at Dartmouth College in Hanover, New Hampshire, at the time, it was an exciting but daunting prospect. Not only was he the sole bachelor’s programme student working alongside senior researchers with years of experience under their belts, he was also the only Black person in the lab. Although Asare’s mentor and colleagues were supportive and encouraging, he felt overwhelmed and out of his depth. “There was a steep learning curve,” he says.

At the time, Asare viewed his struggles as a sign that he didn’t belong in research. This feeling was compounded by the fact that he was surrounded by colleagues who didn’t share his background as a first-generation student from Ghana.

His experience, and those of many like him, is commonly labelled as impostor syndrome — the fear of not being as competent or knowledgeable as other people think, despite objective accomplishments. In a world that often prizes unflinching self-confidence and boldness, impostor syndrome is usually cast as a psychological flaw that the individual needs to ‘fix’. But it can be a natural response to working in a challenging environment or striving towards an ambitious goal, organizational psychologists say.

Impostor syndrome can also be a reaction to systemic bias and exclusion in the workplace, particularly for people from under-represented groups, including women, says Ruchika Malhotra, an inclusion strategist and founder of Candour, a workplace consultancy in Seattle, Washington. The company advises organizations on strategies to create diverse teams and inclusive cultures. One study1 conducted at universities in the United States found that women who work in scientific fields that particularly value intellectual brilliance are more likely to feel like impostors than are their male colleagues.

Much of the discussion about impostor syndrome pathologizes healthy self-doubt and shifts the responsibility onto individuals instead of the environments that exclude and marginalize them in the first place, adds Malhotra. “A lot of the ways that it’s been talked about haven’t been constructive,” she says.

Although it comes with drawbacks, in some situations, impostor syndrome can be beneficial. For instance, it can help people be better prepared and more focused, particularly when they have a long to-do list.

“Impostor thoughts are almost like your superpower when things get pretty overwhelming,” says Basima Tewfik, an organizational psychologist who studies impostor syndrome at Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge.

Looking back, Asare says that his impostor syndrome prompted him to reflect on why he wanted to become a researcher in the first place. It has also made him more conscious of his resilience, how he needs to improve and when to seek help, as well as giving him more empathy. This has made him better able to support younger students and researchers who are feeling out of place. “It became my strength,” says Asare, who is now an oncology researcher and consultant at Dartmouth Hitchcock Medical Center in Lebanon, New Hampshire.

Impostor syndrome was first described as ‘impostor phenomenon’ in a 1978 paper on high-achieving women2 co-authored by psychologists Pauline Clance and Suzanne Imes, both then at Georgia State University in Atlanta. They wrote that people who experience this phenomenon “maintain a strong belief that they are not intelligent; in fact they are convinced that they have fooled anyone who thinks otherwise”.

In the decades since, impostor phenomenon has morphed into a syndrome, even though it isn’t a medical diagnosis, nor is it classified as a psychiatric disorder. A review published in 20233 suggests that around 70% of people will feel unworthy of their accomplishments at some point in their lives. These feelings are even more prevalent in academia, with a 2012 study4 finding that as many as 82% of graduate students experience impostor syndrome to at least some degree. This pattern of thinking often affects high achievers and is associated with lower job satisfaction, hindered performance and burnout. Although some studies, including the 2012 paper, suggest that impostor syndrome affects mostly women and people from other groups under-represented in academia, others argue that it arises in specific situations rather than among particular groups. Relatively few studies have investigated whether commonly cited strategies, such as listing one’s accomplishments and accepting compliments from others, are actually effective.

Impostor syndrome has become a catchphrase in popular culture, with dozens of articles, books and courses describing what it is and how people can overcome it. But in the scientific literature, at least, the exact definition of impostor syndrome, or phenomenon, varies widely. This has created a murky picture of what it really is and how it affects people, says Tewfik. “There are a lot of different ways people describe this phenomenon,” she says. The loose definition has made it easy to confuse impostor syndrome, which causes people to make inferences about what other people think of them, with regular self-doubt, which is more of a personal reflection of your own capabilities, according to Tewfik.

‘Maybe I was never meant to be in science’: how impostor syndrome seizes scientist mothers

‘Maybe I was never meant to be in science’: how impostor syndrome seizes scientist mothers

Much of the research on impostor syndrome has also used measures that have made it difficult to distinguish from other psychological patterns, such as negative affectivity, a personality trait that is linked to a tendency to experience negative emotions such as fear, anxiety and insecurity, adds Tewfik. This crossover might explain why most studies on impostor syndrome have shown only negative outcomes, such as a lack of career planning and low motivation to lead5. “It’s possible that what we’ve been studying is actually something much more akin to fear,” says Tewfik.

This overly negative slant is exacerbated by the fact that many workplaces, including academic ones, place too much emphasis on self-confidence, says Tomas Chamorro-Premuzic, an organizational psychologist at University College London. One 2024 study6 found that workers who display confidence are perceived as more competent and dominant, irrespective of their actual ability.

If impostor syndrome hinders a person’s ability to work or form relationships, it’s usually a symptom of a deeper issue or clinical condition, such as an anxiety disorder. But feeling like you’re about to be ‘found out’ before delivering a big presentation, for example, is usually a sign that you’re being challenged or working outside your comfort zone, says Chamorro-Premuzic. “There is a very healthy degree somewhere that we’re not appreciating,” he adds (see ‘A toolkit for working with impostor syndrome’).

In scientists, impostor thoughts can simply be a by-product of thinking critically and approaching things with a healthy dose of scepticism, says Samantha Sutton, an independent career coach for scientists in Boston, Massachusetts. It’s also often a natural response to working in a high-achieving, competitive environment or towards an ambitious goal and should be normalized instead of treated as a problem to solve, she adds. “If you’re up against something big, you should be scared,” says Sutton. When she communicates this to her clients, they are often relieved to hear that they don’t need to strive for total self-confidence before taking steps towards their goals. “They realize that nothing is wrong,” adds Sutton.

#895. 37 years after fall of Berlin Wall: How divided are Germans?

Three artists share their thoughts on the reunification of East and West Germany. How do they perceive a shared "we" and what gives them cause for optimism?

When the Berlin Wall fell on November 9, 1989, ending East Germany's isolation from the West, the event was celebrated on both sides of the border. Yet, 37 years later, many people on both sides remain deeply skeptical of each other.

Surveys show that only a minority of respondents report feeling a strong sense of community between those from former East and West Germany, and many continue to perceive significant differences.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

We asked three artists from Germany with different perspectives on the history of the country's division to share their views.

Author Lea Streisand was born in 1979 and experienced the fall of the Berlin Wall firsthand while growing up in East Berlin.

In her books and essays, she has returned to her East German upbringing many times, using literature to process it.

The novel "Hufeland, at the corner of Bötzow" (2019, Ullstein), for example, recounts the period of reunification from a child's perspective.

"November 9, 1989, was simply incredible," she told DW. She was 10 years old at the time. When her mother bought her winter boots with the 100 Deutsche Marks she received from the West German state — a welcome gift given to all East German citizens — she was so disappointed that she felt like crying. But later, a friend of her parents' let her buy so many sweets at the supermarket that they lasted until Christmas.

"The disappointment really set in afterwards, with what happened over the course of the following year. It was unbelievable how quickly an entire system was suddenly swept away and a new one built up, as if to say, 'There you go. You're welcome'," Streisand recalled. "I think it was just too fast for people."

The people of East Germany, or the GDR, had brought about the fall of the Berlin Wall themselves through a civil rights movement and numerous demonstrations. For many, however, the goal was not to dissolve the state immediately but to reform it.

Among them was Anke Feuchtenberger, born in 1963 in East Berlin. Her childhood was spent in East Berlin and in the East German region of Western Pomerania, where she now lives again and feels "very much at home."

Today, she teaches at the University of Applied Sciences in Hamburg, meaning she spends time on both sides of the former divide. Feuchtenberger is often described as Germany's most influential comic artist. Her work has also garnered international acclaim.

"Back then, as artists, we tried to bring about a change through posters and flyers — to gain more freedom without immediately abolishing socialism," she explained.

At the time, the fall of the Berlin Wall stirred up mixed feelings in Feuchtenberger: "I soon realized that the creative and revolutionary aspects of our movement were very quickly being smothered by consumerism, and that nationalist tendencies — which had already been noticeable before — were coming to the fore," Feuchtenberger recalled. "That made me afraid."

Meanwhile, for photographic artist Simon Menner, born in 1978 in Emmendingen, in the West German state of Baden-Württemberg, Berlin was very far away. As Menner put it, he experienced the fall of the Berlin Wall as a child in a "rather abstract" way. Today, Berlin is his home.

In his experience, the way films and documentaries portrayed East Germany around the time of reunification was very bleak. "But West Germany in the '80s," he said, "was also bleak and very staid."

This uneven portrayal of the two parts of Germany is an issue that deeply concerns Menner — partly because he unwittingly contributed to it in a small way. Among other things, Menner's work explores the topic of surveillance and how it works.

In the archives of East Germany's Ministry for State Security, or Stasi — which are freely accessible today as part of the National Archives — he discovered a massive collection of photographs that both fascinated and horrified him and which he wanted to bring to the attention of a wider public.

His photo book "Top Secret" (2012, from publisher Hatje Cantz) features a selection of photos that offer a unique insight into the work of the Stasi. Some are eerie, while others are curious or even absurd.

Menner also tried to look into the photo archive of West Germany's Federal Intelligence Service. "I spent a year trying to gain access — without success," he said.

In hindsight, he now finds his artistic project problematic because he believes it is too one-sided, focusing exclusively on East Germany's past.

According to Menner, West Germany's intelligence services in the 1960s were not exactly models of virtue either, and he believes it is "actually high time" to critically examine this part of history as well. In his view, an honest examination of Germany's past as a whole is a prerequisite for genuine reconciliation.

Streisand believes literature can help foster mutual understanding. "Literature opens a window into experiences we haven't had ourselves," she said. "You can immerse yourself in the mind of someone who has had a different life than you have and understand what happened."

Interest in these stories remains strong. In 2023, Feuchtenberger published the nearly 500-page graphic novel "Comrade Cuckoo" (published by Reprodukt), which was the first graphic novel to be nominated for the Leipzig Book Fair Prize in the fiction category.

The story spans a childhood in the fictional East German village of Pritschitanow in the 1960s in the GDR to the post-Reunification era. In it, Feuchtenberger weaves autobiographical memories of her upbringing with fantastical and fictional elements.

The artist said she was surprised "that, so long after the fall of the wall, my stories have sparked such great interest in the West."

In particular, the fact that the main character, Kerstin, rarely sees her parents because they both work full-time is a topic that often comes up at readings. In the GDR, everyone had the right to work, she said. At the same time, it was a civic duty.

Could the West German interest in this stem from the fact that full-time employment for both parents has long been less common in the West? It's possible, said Feuchtenberger.

When looking toward their shared future, the two East German women are more optimistic than Menner, from West Germany.

"In Berlin, I often don't even notice anymore whether I'm in the West or the East," said Menner. "But when it comes to sociopolitical issues, politicians should listen to older and younger people more closely," he added, referring to the recent election successes of far-right Alternative for Germany, or AfD . "Otherwise, things are going to get difficult in the near future."

"It's very important to step outside our own bubble because people all over the world are facing problems. Constantly focusing on this German-German divide that has emerged between the groups doesn't help," said Feuchtenberger.

"For me personally, the whole issue of borders has somehow dissolved," she explained. This is due in no small part to the many trips abroad that have taken her to various places around the world.

Moreover, in her hometown near the Polish border, she observes how animals couldn't care less about the border. "They come from the east and the west and do whatever they want," she said. That's why she also gave "Comrade Cuckoo" the working title "A German Animal in a German Forest," "because I found the absurdity of an animal having a nationality so funny."

"This East-West thing — our children won't have any interest in it at all," said Streisand. "Young people don't care where their parents come from. Can I get a job that will support a family? Do I have to go to war? Right now, completely different things are relevant."

This article was originally written in German.

#894. 10 games, 0 points & 30 goals conceded - why Charlton are struggling

Ashleigh Neville joined Charlton from Leicester City in the summer

Charlton Athletic achieved the unthinkable last season when they earned promotion to the Women's Super League - but it has been a harsh introduction.

After 10 games in the top flight, Karen Hills' side are yet to pick up a point and have scored just five goals, conceding 30.

They have already lost to the other promoted sides - Birmingham City and Crystal Palace - and are six points adrift at the bottom of the table.

The club expected a tough challenge as they made the jump up to the WSL for the first time but the results have still hit them hard.

"I'm trying everything I can," manager Hills said following their 2-0 defeat by West Ham last weekend.

That result came a week after Charlton's 3-2 loss at Crystal Palace where they had been leading with 16 minutes to go.

So is it time to consider relegation, even in November, or is there still hope for Charlton to turn things around?

Charlton pipped better resourced teams in the WSL 2 last season, eventually beating top-flight side Leicester City in a play-off to secure promotion.

An incredible 27-game unbeaten run ended in March but was founded on an effective defensive structure and often heroics by goalkeeper Sophie Whitehouse.

However, the step up has proved difficult with inexperience and tight finances standing in the way.

Statistically, Charlton rank bottom in the WSL for average possession (30%), shots on target (17), passing accuracy (66%) and successful passes (1,689).

They have conceded nine times from set-pieces - the most in the WSL - and 14 of their total goals against have come in either the first or final 15 minutes in games.

The only other sides to lose their first 10 games in a WSL season are Doncaster Rovers Belles in 2016 and Yeovil Town in 2017-18. The Belles went on to win just one game as they were relegated, while Yeovil failed to win any, drawing two and finishing bottom, only avoiding relegation because of a league restructure.

Experienced defender Ashleigh Neville, who joined Charlton from Leicester City in the summer, told BBC Sport: "We knew it was going to be a tough start to the season.

"I was really excited to embrace that challenge. It's been difficult with results but when you look at the first game compared to now, I'd like to hope that people can see we're trying to build something.

"We're trying the hardest we can off the pitch to get to terms with how quick the game is compared to the WSL 2 and the quality of players we're up against.

"But it's still a joy to come into work and people are wanting to be better, asking how they can improve and move forward."

This month, manager Hills insisted Charlton "will never throw the towel in" but admitted results are "hurting" the club.

Neville added: "It is not at the forefront of things but we've been really unlucky with the injuries that we've had in our attacking line.

"We're lacking in confidence going forward, and creativity for what we can actually provide.

"It's a vicious circle. If you haven't got confidence because you're losing games, how do you still get that confidence in games where we need it the most?"

Whitehouse's penalty masterclass sends Charlton into WSL

How WSL 2 title contenders Charlton are defying the odds

Karen Hills was a player at Charlton Athletic before retiring in 2007

Charlton are one of only three clubs without Premier League male counterparts to offer financial backing in the WSL and that restricts their freedom in recruitment.

It has not helped that summer signing Linda Lif Boama suffered a serious knee injury in September, defender Grace Johnston was ruled out in October and Paula Partido had to return to parent club London City Lionesses for knee surgery.

Charlotte Newsham, who played a key role in their WSL 2 promotion run, was also sidelined by an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury before the play-off victory.

While Charlton sought out shrewd signings in the summer, rivals Birmingham City were able to spend six-figure sums on Manchester United duo Lisa Naalsund and Millie Turner.

The Blues also broke their club record in January - a reported Â£316,000 fee for Wilma Leidhammar - while Oceane Hurtre was signed last summer to boost their second-tier title hopes and has now scored seven goals in 10 WSL games.

Fellow promoted club Palace picked up four-time WSL winner Bethany England and one of the WSL 2's standout players Lexi Lloyd-Smith in the summer.

"WSL 2 teams have to be even more ready for the WSL while they're still in the WSL 2 so that when they do make that jump, it's not a huge gap," said Hills.

"The gap is continuing to get bigger and you see some of the players the top teams have brought in and the finances they have.

"It's a big challenge for us. We're finding that out on a weekly basis."

Charlton benefited from the WSL's expansion this summer to 14 teams from 12 as organisers try to bridge the gap between the leagues and to increase the number of matches.

It was well-received by fans and those within the game, but Hills says it will still take time for WSL 2 clubs to catch up.

"If you look at the bottom three teams [in the table], it's all the newly-promoted teams. The level that we're coming into is already very well established."

Neville added: "I think the financial side plays a massive part. We do our bit where we can. But it's hard to bring in the experienced players you need."

#893. Arsenal’s Lisa Baum: ‘I believe in us. I think it’s all about the small margins’

Germany forward on her new life in London and drawing strength from the memory of her late brother, Dennis

Lisa Baum is 19, for the next few days at least, but you wouldn’t know it. The Germany forward plays with a maturity that explains why she was handed her Arsenal debut in their opening game of the season, less than two months after joining.

Baum had been told that the 2025 European champions had a vision for her but that coming in as a young player she would have to be patient. Ten minutes into her debut against Brighton, in Crawley, the young winger scored what would be the winning goal.

“It was unbelievable,” says Baum, speaking in a small meeting room at Arsenal’s London Colney training ground with a maturity that matches her play. “Everything just went so quick. I just shot, my brain was just switched off, it just came out.”

That win kickstarted Arsenal’s season but it quickly stalled. In the league, the team went five games without a win. After a 2-0 defeat by OL Lyonnes in the Champions League on Thursday night, Arsenal have five wins from their opening 15 games. It is far from the season they, or many others, envisaged.

Sunday’s final home game of the year, against West Ham, offers an opportunity to take some positivity into the international break, after which Arsenal face three away fixtures before the winter pause.

“I believe in us,” says Baum. “I think it’s all about the small margins. Sometimes it’s luck, sometimes it’s in the final decision-making, sometimes it’s how close we are to a goal that doesn’t go in. But we work really hard in every training session and on trying to keep ourselves up mentally and physically. We’re trying to push through the barrier that we maybe have right now, but we get a lot of trust from the staff and coaches. Everybody really believes in each other and I think it’s not going to take long before we’re through this part of the journey.”

Overall, Arsenal have not been playing particularly badly. They have been creating chances and dominating games but struggling to translate that into goals and points. In October, Baum earned a first senior Germany call-up and made her debut off the bench at half-time against Australia, having previously featured for teams from the under-16s to under-23s.

The Liverpool head coach, Gareth Taylor, says Pro Ref has accepted it made an error in disallowing a goal his side thought they had scored during this month's 2-1 defeat by Arsenal at Anfield.

The Women’s Super League game was level at 1-1 when Jenna Clark tucked the ball into the net after ­Arsenal had failed to clear a corner, but the assistant referee disallowed the goal for offside against Vivien ­Endemann. Replays showed the delivery had been ­inadvertently played off an Arsenal foot rather than being a deliberate forward pass from the home side. There is no VAR in the WSL.

Taylor, whose side host Chelsea in the WSL on Saturday, said on Friday: “We have had an acceptance of a mistake from the corner that we scored from, where we should be 2-1 up at half-time. [There was] no apology, but we accept that there was an error made on their part and that game can look different.” Tom Garry

Baum moved to Germany when she was four. Born to a Tanzanian mother and German father, she spent her first years in Dar es Salaam in Tanzania. They swapped a city with a population of about four million for Ahrensbök, a municipality with a population of just over 8,000 near the Baltic coast. “I think my mum had the hardest time out of us in the family, with the move to Germany,” she says. Baum says she and her brother, Dennis, “learned to adapt easily”.

Baum doesn’t remember her years on the east coast of Africa but when she went back three or four years ago, some sort of memory was triggered. “It was a feeling, or feelings,” she says. “It was so good to grow up there. It was warm, it was the beautiful beaches, it was having all your family around. I was in kindergarten or I was in the water a lot – I love to swim.”

She started playing football after the move to northern Germany, desperate to copy Dennis. “My father played football when he was younger – he was a goalkeeper – but he stopped when he didn’t really enjoy it any more. My mum wasn’t a big fan of me playing; she dressed me like a girly girl, with princess dresses and that kind of stuff, but I was never really like that at that age. I always wanted to follow my older brother – I wanted to wear his clothes. He started playing football before me and I wanted to be like him.”

No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football

Baum would play on the side of the pitch at her brother’s club until a parent said she should be playing too. After playing with various local teams she joined Hamburg’s academy. She worked her way into the first team and they won promotion to the second tier in her first season. In the 2024-25 season they reached the DFB-Pokal semi-finals and the top flight. Baum moved to RB Leipzig and scored five goals in 27 games before Arsenal swooped.

“Everything was just so quick,” she says of the move to London. Training required getting used to: “Everything was so sharp, everything was technically excellent, like 10 out of 10. I was quite nervous and had some clumsy actions.”

The transfer also involved swapping an average attendance last season of 1,651 for one of 33,808. “It’s unbelievable,” says Baum of playing at the Emirates Stadium. “I had only played in a big stadium once before. You can’t even believe how much the fans give you when you step on the pitch. There’s so much support, that of course we need in this current time. I think Arsenal is a club that holds on to us, on to the team, and gives us a lot of strength.”

Look closely at Baum’s left wrist when she plays and you will usually see a strip of white tape around it. Sometimes it has something written on it. She’s done it “since that day” – the day in 2022 when Dennis died in a car accident, aged 17.

The brother that inspired her on to a pitch is with her on it at the highest level. “The next time I was on the football pitch, I just felt I wanted to do that,” she says. “I feel like it’s given me a different kind of strength and confidence. Sometimes I don’t write anything, but it’s about just having the physical feeling that he is with me.”

#892. 'They looked like a team again' - Hearts roar back with Dundee demolition

Hearts are now the highest scorers in the Premiership with 34 goals from 13 games

"I've been in football 37 years and I've never experienced anything like that," said a hugely dispirited Steven Pressley after Dundee were demolished 8-0 at home by Hearts on Saturday.

The jubilant victors can top that span of time by quite a distance given they are celebrating their biggest away win since they began playing league football in the 1890s, a result which also happens to be Dundee's record home defeat.

It was just the third 8-0 game in Scottish top-flight history, after Rangers crushed Clyde in 1931 and Celtic hammered Hamilton in 1988.

The eight at Dens Park came from 14 efforts on target and an expected goals (xG) of just 3.5.

Ruthless Hearts put eight past ramshackle 10-man Dundee

There were some fine finishes, a deft first-time effort from Sabah Kerjota being the pick of the bunch, a lot of shoddy defending, and a red card for the hosts before the hour with the score at 4-0.

Just the tonic for Hearts after three defeats in a week prior to the international break, including a League Cup semi-final derby and a shellacking from Falkirk which ended their 19-month unbeaten league streak at Tynecastle.

"They really looked like a team again," enthused former club hero John Robertson on Sportsound. "The rotations were good, the passing was good. The guys coming off the bench wanted to be part of this and they just kept going and going."

Another ex-Hearts player, Michael Stewart, called it the "perfect evening".

"To come here and win was the most important thing, but to do it in such a fashion is as good a reset as you're ever going to get," he said on Premier Sports.

Hearts are the Premiership's top scorers with 34 from 13 outings.

Add goals against and you have a whopping tally of 56, with five conceded at home to Falkirk last time and seven shipped at Celtic Park last month.

This was just a third league blank for Wouter Vrancken's defence.

"It sounds crazy after scoring eight, but the clean sheet is maybe the most important thing," added Robertson. "They just haven't had enough of them."

Reflecting on the biggest win of his career, the Belgian appeared to agree, telling BBC Sport Scotland: "What actually pleased me the most was at six or seven when Dundee were countering, nine players were sprinting back to fight for a clean sheet.

Hearts returned from the previous international break with a 5-0 win over St Mirren before the heavy loss to Celtic and Vrancken is certainly not getting carried away with nine more games coming over the next 30 days, beginning at home to Monaco in the Conference League on Thursday.

"We had talks before our days off, they were really honest and open," he revealed.

"It was good to hear but you have to take ownership of it on the pitch. You can talk as much as you want but if you can't show it on the pitch it doesn't mean anything.

"When you do it like this it's the first step. But it's only the first step, only one game and we have to try to bring more.

"It was ruthless but the schedule is also ruthless â but we got a good boost from tonight."

Having gone into the international break on the back off those three successive losses, Hearts fans may have been apprehensive.

After all, Dundee had lost just once at Dens Park all season, back in August.

However, the hosts were abject, allowing Hearts so much room.

"Every aspect of our performance was below par," bemoaned Pressley. "We looked unmotivated and lacking edge.

"Of course the sending off made the second half very difficult, but we didn't do the things that are normally associated with our performance.

"We weren't gritty enough in our defending, we didn't fill the spaces we normally do. We normally defend in a particularly strong manner, but we didn't do that.

"I can only apologise. My thoughts are that it's on myself. It's my responsibility to make sure you see a motivated Dundee team, it is my responsibility to make sure we are tactically sound, it is my responsibility to make sure they show grit and determination and not go under like we did.

"I had a little sense we haven't been quite on it over the last couple of weeks but I never expected that and I take ownership."

#891. 'I persuaded my club to give me a job as a content creator'

If someone would've said to me I'd be doing this as a job when I was 12, I wouldn't have believed them.

My name's Jacob. I'm a content creator, and I work with Bolton Wanderers.

My role here at Bolton is coming up with new ideas for social media, to try new concepts, filming stuff, and then posting them onto Bolton's pages and trying to help people follow the club. In my opinion, I think it's one of the funnest jobs in football, and it's brilliant.

Right. Welcome to Bolton, Larra. I hope I said that right. I'm going to teach you some Bolton twang to help you settle in.

My passion for football when I was growing up started at a very young age. My dad used to take me to the football matches, and I got my very first season ticket when I was five years old in the 2010/11 season, when Bolton was in the Premiership. Being something I loved as a kid, to turn it into my job is amazing.

I work here at least two days a week, obviously filming content, producing content,and then on match day, I'll be filming mostly with fans, and I love it.

As a town? Well, for us, it's lovely. Yeah.

Mondays, meetings. We have the marketing meeting, so that gives you an idea of what the week holds, what I'm going to do on a match day with the fans. And then in the week, I either film in with players, retail, commercial,whatever department needs help producing videos.

Some of the skills I use, I think one of them's got to be communication. You've got to be able to talk to people, talk to fans, and if you're watching this and you're a bit shy, or you think you can't communicate with people as well, I was like that inhigh school, so you learn it as you get older. But working in football, you've got to be adaptable because one minute you're doing a new signing, next minute you're working with the players, next minute it's a match day, next minute the season's over.

I'd say another one is being creative. That's probably the most important one because without being creative, you won't be able to put a video together.

So when I was 16 in high school, that's where my journey started. I did videos, which got me a number of followers. I always struggled in the classroom side in high school, but creating content and creating ideas and being creative, I was always really, really good at in high school, whether that would be doing something drama-related or English, writing, creating stories. I always knew I had a passion for creative pieces of work and being able to now do it as a job, it suits me down to the ground.

I didn't go to college. I didn't go to uni. I left high school with no GCSEs, but I've always had a real passion for football, so that's how I got in contact with Bolton Wanderers. I started doing some videos here at Bolton with the fans and that, and then it turned into going to the training ground and filming with the players, working with the commercial team, retail team, all the different departmentsaround the football club to eventually getting a paid role in football.

I think don't wait for an opportunity to come to you. Get out there and try. If you're good at it, it does then sometimes lead into getting a role there. But if it doesn't, then you've also created a portfolio working with different people, different businesses, different companies, and it's really good for your CV and for future opportunities with different companies.

The highlight of my career so far, probably looking back, being resilient enough to create my own career path in doing something I love.

When you score this season, you might be chuffed.

If you're passionate about football, you're a bit creative, and you're good in front of the camera, content creation infootball might be a job for you.

To find out what other careers you can have in football, explore the BBC Bitesize Follow Your Passion collection.

Making videos with fans and players at his local football club is all in a day's work for Jacob.

He's a content creator for Bolton Wanderers FC, coming up with new ideas for social media, filming videos and posting them onto official pages. The aim is to encourage people to follow the club.

There are many different ways to develop a career in football content creation, from apprenticeships to freelance work and full-time employment. It isn't just about making videos - content creators need to understanding their audience, respond to analytics and adapt material for different platforms

Jacob works as a content creator for Bolton Wanderers and his career progression has followed this path:

Voluntary work at Bolton --> Professional content creator

While it might look simple, he's had to be resilient - and one of the biggest obstacles he faced was convincing Bolton to create his role. "Don't wait for an opportunity to come to you," he says. "If you're good at it, it does then sometimes lead into getting a role. If it doesn't, you've created a portfolio and it's really good for your CV and future opportunities."

Jacob says salaries can range from Â£26,000 to around Â£40,000 for roles like his. Like him, some content creators start by doing it as a hobby while they improve their skills. While some content creators are full-time employees, many are freelancers so their average salaries can be variable.

Find out more about the role of a content creator below. Content creation roles can come under a range of titles including social media manager or content manager.

You could get into this role via a college course (to get practical skills in video editing and production, or a T Level in Marketing), an apprenticeship, volunteering, short private training courses and also teaching yourself.

This information is a guide and is constantly changing. Please check the National Careers Service website for the latest information and all the qualifications needed and the GOV.UK website for more on T-levels.

For careers advice in all parts of the UK visit: National Careers Service (England), nidirect (Northern Ireland), My World of Work (Scotland) and Careers Wales (Wales).

Bitesize Careers, in partnership with The Open University, has launched the Follow Your Passion campaign, exploring how you can draw on your passions and interests to find your future jobs, with the focus on football.

From content creation to computer game design, nutrition to number-crunching, check out the Bitesize Careers Follow Your Passion collection for loads of inspiring careers content.

#890. Brighton are rocking the Premier League elite. But can they mount a title tilt?

A combination of smart analytics, a young manager and players hand-picked for their particular skills has the Seagulls flying high

They lined up in sky‑blue shirts, white shorts. A combined value of £327m. Enzo Fernández, Ayyoub Bouaddi and Elliot Anderson were starting their first match together in Manchester City’s midfield.

But it was a Brighton midfielder who made the game’s first decisive contribution. Yasin Ayari slotted the ball home. The away crowd at the Etihad Stadium roared, then watched their team defend relentlessly, securing Brighton’s first league victory away to City.

It was 31 October 2026. There are dangers in reading too much into a single result this early in the season. Teams are still finding their rhythm, new signings bedding in. But this result packed some punch.

If spending decided football matches, Brighton & Hove Albion should not be competing with, let alone beating, Manchester City, who sign established stars for astronomical fees and wages. Erling Haaland is paid £525,000 a week.

According to an independent commission, to circumvent the Premier League’s spending limits, which restrict a club’s losses, City artificially inflated their commercial revenues by £830m between 2009 and 2018. Brighton, by contrast, tend to buy potential, scouring the market for undervalued talent, often in less prominent leagues. After developing them and benefiting from their performances, the club sell them for profits.

They paid just £3.5m for Ayari, offering him about £10,000 a week, and paired him in midfield with Chema Andrés and Pascal Gross, signed for a combined fee of less than £25m.

The most remarkable thing about Brighton’s win was that it wasn’t really a shock. In September, they dismantled Arsenal, the Premier League champions and favourites for the title. As they prepare for Sunday’s match at Hull, they are second in the league, sandwiched between Arsenal and City, and have scored more goals than anyone else in the division. How, then, do Brighton excel on the pitch without haemorrhaging money? And is there a ceiling to what they can achieve?

On a crisp late October morning, I drove to Brighton in search of answers. Deep inside the Amex, the club’s stadium, I met Paul Barber, Brighton’s CEO, a cheerful man who speaks with the calmness of someone with nowhere else to be.

“Being the size of club that we are, we had to find a way of being competitive that was probably different to any of the other bigger clubs that we were aiming to compete with,” Barber said, “because their revenues are always going to be higher: bigger stadiums, more established sponsorship models, bigger stars, bigger brands.”

Hours before Brighton beat City, Chelsea had beaten Manchester United. In their respective midfields were Moisés Caicedo and Carlos Baleba, whom Brighton had signed for a combined fee of less than £30m and sold for about £180m. “It’s those trading profits that are effectively the core of the Brighton model,” Barber explained.

Most clubs recruit and develop talent, I pointed out, but few do it better than Brighton. Who, outside Ecuador, had heard of Caicedo before he signed for Brighton in 2021? Two years later, the world’s biggest clubs were competing for his signature. The same can be said of dozens of others, among them Marc Cucurella and Alexis Mac Allister. One diamond exits, another enters. Caicedo replaced Yves Bissouma in central midfield. Baleba replaced Caicedo. The same applies to the dugout. Before joining Brighton, Fabian Hürzeler was coaching St Pauli in Germany; before him, Roberto De Zerbi had been at Shakhtar Donetsk.

Barber grinned. “There’s a myth that we have this secret supply of players,” he said. The explanation is Jamestown Analytics, a sports analytics company founded by the club’s owner, Tony Bloom, as an offshoot of Starlizard, the gambling consultancy he established in 2006. Just as Starlizard uses proprietary modelling to identify mispriced odds in betting markets, Jamestown uses algorithms to identify underdeveloped football talents. “They’re all out there,” Barber said. “The data just enables Brighton to home in on them faster and earlier.”

When I asked for more detail about how the system works, Barber fiddled with his watch. Jamestown tracks a vast number of performance indicators for every player competing in professional football, many of which aren’t captured by other data providers. “Every action that players are taking on a football pitch is being looked at, measured and codified in some way,” he said.

When the club identify a position to strengthen, they draw up a list of attributes for the ideal player. Some are universal to the position: a centre-back generally needs to be tall. Others depend on the specific coach and their style of football.

Later, when I spoke to Hürzeler, the head coach, he explained that the data had to reflect the specific demands of his playing system. “A player needs to have some basic things that fit our style of play, so if a player doesn’t want to have the ball then it’s difficult to play in our team. If a player doesn’t want to press high then it’s difficult to play in our team. These are just two examples.”

One reason Brighton recruited Luka Vuskovic in July 2026 was because Hürzeler wanted a mobile centre-back. Reflecting on the City match, Barber recalled seeing Vuskovic pushing “so far forward that you’d have thought he was a right midfielder”. It was the sort of mobility Hürzeler’s system demanded, and Jamestown had identified.

Before Brighton’s victory over City, I met Mike Cave, the club’s sporting director, at the Lowry hotel in Manchester. A few of the Brighton players wandered around in club tracksuits. Cave wore a suit and tie and his hair was slicked back. He was telling me it was a big day without saying it.

Brighton’s recruitment advantage lies not simply in the quality and quantity of the data at their disposal, he said, but in their ability to interpret it and trust what it tells them. “You could have the best data in the world but if you’re not accustomed to using it, and if you’re not clear about how it informs your decision-making process, then it’s just a lot of data that doesn’t move the dial.”

The power of data is that it strips away emotions and preconceptions. When watching games, Hürzeler said he often identifies a player he thinks is performing well and texts Cave, only to learn that the numbers don’t support his impression. The conversation ends. “The numbers have to be right otherwise we have no chance of getting a player in.”

Conversely, the data identifies players he might not otherwise have considered – such as Diego Gómez, the Paraguayan signed from Inter Miami in 2024. Despite the strength of Gómez’s underlying numbers, the club had a free run at signing him. Cave suggested this reflected a misconception that players in MLS aren’t equipped to play in the Premier League. “What the data has allowed us to do is step away from some of those biases and just be clear on what the evidence tells us, to look at the signal rather than the noise.”

But identifying a player who can perform for Brighton is different from identifying one who will, Cave said. The club’s requirements are so specific that the data typically identifies only around five candidates, Hürzeler says, and fewer still are affordable. Of those remaining, the recruitment team and Hürzeler will speak to anyone with experience of them – players, coaches and sponsors – to learn more about their character and personality, and prepare dossiers. Together, they’ll identify a primary target and make a move. “It’s not like I get a list and then decide which players; it’s something we all decide together,” said Hürzeler.

As Barber explained: “The more we can find out about a player’s character the less risk there is of that player being rejected like a bad organ transplant.” There’s no exhaustive list of desirable characteristics, he added, but “coachability” is key. Brighton’s model hinges on players having the capacity to improve, and the best indication is their drive to do so. “The biggest element of coachability is attitude.”

Hürzeler asks himself: “What are they willing to give for their development? Are they willing to suffer?” He’s convinced this desire is innate. “These are things I can’t control.”

Conversations with people around Gómez painted a picture of “a boy that is clearly trying to get absolutely everything out of his career”, said Cave. But sometimes the qualities Brighton are looking for aren’t so obvious. Whereas the data is objective, says Barber, references are “someone’s opinion”. It’s challenging to know how much weight to give a single person’s negative judgment, particularly when it conflicts with other opinions, without dismissing it altogether. “Sometimes when you want to sign somebody you can subjectively screen out the negativity because you want them, and the data says you need them.”

Beyond character, the team consider a player’s ability to settle into a new country, and whether their partner will, too. Once Brighton make an offer, the player is normally keen to join, in Barber’s experience, because they know it can lead to a move to “potentially bigger things”. The selling club is often receptive because there are rarely any other comparable offers on the table.

But this has been changing, says Barber. Brighton’s success means their interest in a player “alerts other clubs to that talent”, creating competition. Selling clubs, meanwhile, have reason to believe that the player “has the potential to be valued for a lot more”. Increasingly, then, Brighton are having to pay more, making “our ability to trade profitably ever harder”.

Even if a deal can be agreed, it doesn’t always represent good business. As Cave explained: “You’re dealing with human beings, in a complex system and a complex game, so you will never have a 100% strike record.”

Asked what Brighton looks for in recruits, Gordon Greer, who played for the club from 2010 to 2016, was quick to answer: “high potential”. But that potential rarely means they’re ready to slot into the first‑team. Today, as Brighton’s pathway development manager, Greer’s job is to bridge that gap.

To understand how Greer does this, I joined him for coffee at the Lowry. He told me that he begins planning a player’s development while the club are still negotiating his signing. “In the buildup to us signing him, we’ll start to analyse him … what’s his strengths, what’s his weaknesses … where do we think we can help?” Once he’s met the player and understood their ambitions, he turns that assessment into a development plan.

To begin, Greer explained, he asked himself: “What are this player’s limiting factors to play for Brighton?” Sometimes the answer lies off the pitch. Hürzeler requires his players to speak English. It helps embed his playing principles by allowing the players to transmit them to each other. “We want to have a common language, so they can coach each other on the pitch,” he explained. Other times the shortcomings are more directly related to football, such as back‑post defending. A typical one is physicality; Hürzeler’s counter-pressing requires repeated sprints and many recruits would risk injury if they were thrown into the first team. “The game is so fast, and the intensity is crazy,” Jack Hinshelwood, who made his first‑team debut in 2023, has said.

One pathway for development is the under-21s team, Greer says, but the physical demands of the game fall short of those in the Premier League. Hinshelwood, who came through the under-21s, suffered a stress fracture in his foot after a few top-flight games. “You need time to adapt,” he said. In Greer’s view, the level doesn’t challenge most recruits enough for them to learn. “We want to put them in a position where they’re stretched enough that they’re uncomfortable but they’ve got enough success that they’re doing things that they enjoy.”

An alternative is the loan market. Since 2018–19, Brighton have agreed more than 20 loan deals in each campaign. Playing time is an important consideration when arranging a loan, Greer explains, because a player’s value can drop if they’re not playing often. But he also considers the location, manager, formation and quality of the pitch. Position is crucial, too. Sending a striker to a team near the bottom of their league, where they’re likely to be living off scraps, can see their confidence and value drop, but sending a defender into the same environment can accelerate their development with repeated defensive situations. “You’re trying to get to a point where they’re impacting the game.”

A successful loan addresses a player’s limitations. “You’re trying to expose someone to something totally different,” Greer added. In 2017, Ben White – now of Arsenal and England – was loaned to Newport County to improve the “urgency in his defending”.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

“The game model was end‑to-end, back-to-front, League Two, where you’re up against it,” Greer added. In 2024, Ibrahim Osman, shortly after signing from Nordsjælland in Denmark, went to Feyenoord, a possession-based team, to develop his technical game. “Physically, he was a beast, but he was quite untidy,” said Greer.

Throughout a loan, each player is continually reassessed. Those ready are brought into Hürzeler’s first team. If they’re not, another spell elsewhere might be arranged. But if their development has stalled for too long, they’ll be encouraged to leave permanently. That was the case with Leo Østigård, a Norway international signed from Molde in 2018. He was a skilled defender but he “wasn’t good enough on the ball”, Greer said. His development slowed down during a loan at Coventry, and then, at Stoke, it became “clear he wasn’t going to be for us”.

Rather than continuing to work on Østigård’s weaknesses, the club sought to maximise his strengths. A loan was arranged at Genoa, a defensive team where Østigård would shine. A year later, he signed for Napoli. “We tried everything but it didn’t work,” Greer said, “so we thought: ‘How do we create as much value as possible?’”

After speaking to Barber, I headed to Brighton’s training base, a short drive away from the Amex, to meet Hürzeler. Academy players milled around outside, while the first team was elsewhere preparing to face Getafe in the Conference League, a competition Brighton are being tipped to win.

I noticed a mural bearing the words: “Challenge the Establishment,” a reference to the so-called big six clubs. A member of staff pointed out that the mural had been Hürzeler’s idea, but the philosophy it exhibits has existed since Bloom took over the club in 2009. Brighton, the member of staff whispered to me, saw themselves as the “antidote” to big-spending clubs such as City.

Before Hürzeler and I sat down in the press conference room, another journalist asked him whether he thought Brighton could win the title. He dismissed the question. His focus was improving the team, he said. He suggested to me, however, that victories such as that over City were the fruits of his work developing the squad and an environment that allows talents to excel. “If you work with players for a longer time, you get used to each other and they get more and more of your principles.”

Hürzeler tells me he relies on older players who embody these principles, such as Lewis Dunk and Pascal Gross. At 33, Hürzeler is younger than both, and became the youngest permanent manager in Premier League history when he was appointed in 2024. When you’re developing raw talents from abroad, while constantly selling and bringing in new players, you need a core group to “build the right culture”. Hinshelwood told me he has experienced this first-hand: “I remember watching their habits every day, how they live their lives, how they’re training, what they’re doing in the gym, how they’re communicating, and I learned so much just by watching them.”

Hürzeler also emphasised the importance of tailoring the support players receive. “You can’t treat a player like Yankuba Minteh who is coming from [the] Gambia the same as a player like Lewis Dunk, who comes from England,” he said. He wants to cultivate an environment in which, as he put it, players, “no matter which age, no matter from where they are coming from, can express themselves”.

To that end, Hürzeler appointed Mike Anthony, who spent 14 years working with New Zealand Rugby, as head of player development and high performance – a new role. One of Anthony’s priorities, he said, has been giving the players more responsibility. Players and the coaches increasingly “lead the programme together”, with players invited to lead discussions.

“They don’t want to just execute things, they want to be valued, they want to be appreciated, they want to be heard by us coaches,” Hürzeler said. “If you don’t give them ownership and responsibility off the pitch, how can you expect them to take responsibility for their own execution on the pitch? It’s not possible.”

A key part of his role, Hürzeler told me, is listening to his players. It helps them perform, and makes him a better coach. He was reminded of this in February 2025, when there were calls for him to lose his job after a poor run that included a 7-0 defeat at Nottingham Forest. James Milner and Danny Welbeck suggested he was overcomplicating his messaging around counter-pressing. Taking their advice on board, he made changes that helped turn things around. “It was definitely one reason why we turned around the results.”

Asked why Brighton have such a strong record for developing talent, Hinshelwood smiled: “You’re allowed to make mistakes, not effort mistakes, or applying yourself badly, but if you make a technical mistake you know you’ve got 10 other players who want you to try things,” he said.

Hürzeler also credited the club’s summer recruitment with this season’s success. Yet Brighton had sold Jan Paul van Hecke to Tottenham and Baleba to United, I pointed out. How could a club expect to improve while selling their best players?

Although he often tries to prevent departures by convincing Bloom not to sell, Hürzeler said he has no final say. “I can’t control whether a player gets a big offer and Tony wants to accept this offer.” But he’s come to see departures as an opportunity to revitalise the squad with new profiles. “When you sign for Brighton, you know that it’s part of the identity, so automatically you have the mindset that you have to deal with these things.”

Being transparent about the club’s model with coaches is a crucial component in their success, according to Barber, but even then it can create tensions. The decision to sell Caicedo was one reason De Zerbi departed, as was the Italian’s insistence on big-name signings rather than trusting the data. It’s no different with supporters, Barber said: “Sometimes when a big player leaves a club and the fans are blindsided by that, it creates this bigger sense of injustice, anger, disappointment.”

Barber also explains that he must go to great lengths to keep costs down. “The difference between what we bring in and what we spend is what we put out on the pitch.” The club’s use of experienced players such as Dunk is ultimately driven by financial constraints. They can’t afford to sign players in their prime, either in transfer fees or wages, so rely on players a little past their prime to counterbalance the inexperience of their younger recruits. “They’re providing that level of experience of a 27-, 28-, 29-year-old, albeit four or five years later, but at a much lower cost.”

Brighton also use data to identify and recruit coaches whose philosophy aligns with the existing squad, minimising the need to overhaul the squad to fit a new style of football. Hürzeler was identified in large part because the numbers showed he could build on the players he inherited. “Revolutions cost a lot of money,” Barber said. “If you can match the coach that you’re bringing into the squad that you’ve got, the cost of change is minimal.”

The final part of the model is knowing when to sell. Barber tries to have a replacement through the door before letting a player go. It becomes trickier to negotiate a fee for a replacement when the selling club knows Brighton have just sold a player for £100m. Barber told me he delayed selling Caicedo until he was confident Baleba could step up. “We felt Carlos had a lot of potential that we could help to realise quite quickly … he’s a quick learner and quite raw, but at the same time you could see rapid improvements in him.”

But other factors matter too, such as whether a player still has room to develop, and therefore increase his value further; the state of the market; and the risk that turning down an offer might jeopardise the chance of a future sale. “If there is a dearth of central midfielders at the moment, maybe now is the time to sell because there will be a significant premium because there are no other options.”

Barber adds that refusing to sell Caicedo to Arsenal in January 2023 was easier because other clubs wanted him in the summer. “Not doing the deal didn’t affect our ability to do the deal with Liverpool and then Chelsea the following summer.”

In their last match before the November international break, Brighton beat Brentford and leapfrogged City. They’d progressed in Europe too: a goal from Malick Yalcouyé, a £6m signing from ​​IFK Göteborg, had beaten Getafe. Outside the ground, fans were dreaming of titles. Barber said he hoped they would not have to wait much longer. “We now need to take the next step and put some silverware on the table.”

But if Brighton are to compete for major trophies, I wondered, will they have to invest more heavily in players, and keep them in their prime? Can the club’s current model allow them to become part of the establishment, rather than simply challenging it?

The club are already adapting, says Barber. The signing of Vuskovic for a club record £46m demonstrates an appetite for talents better equipped to immediately contribute to the first team. “Those players are already at a level of transfer fee that we wouldn’t have contemplated, and 10 years ago we wouldn’t have even considered.” As Jamestown’s algorithm improves, Barber says, he’s hopeful it will become easier for the club to invest these sorts of sums in players, because the risk of getting the assessment wrong will be lower.

But Barber believes player trading is likely to stay as the core of the club’s strategy, partly because they are good at it, but also because they need the revenue. “There’s always going to be this gap [in commercial sales and ticket revenue] so the need for us to trade will always be there.” Even if they did decide to keep players such as Baleba and Van Hecke, would they be able to? As much as a title or two might make it easier to convince top players to stay, Barber said he struggles to envisage a time when they’ll be able to compete with the bigger clubs on wages.

And even if Brighton could one day afford to retain their best players, would it make them less attractive to the next generation of recruits, who might no longer see the club as a stepping stone on the way to the so-called establishment? Could the club become so successful that the prices of their targets rise beyond what they can afford? Might the model self-cannibalise?

Hürzeler tells me he reflects on these same questions. “It’s interesting, this discussion, because these kinds of discussions we also have in the building.” When we spoke on the phone before the Hull match, I brought up Hearts, who have partnered with Jamestown and came close to winning the Scottish title in May for the first time since 1960, challenging the Celtic-Rangers duopoly. I asked whether this gave him the belief that Brighton could go one step further and break the big clubs’ stranglehold.

“Of course, you see this as motivation for what is possible,” he said. He revealed a belief that he can lift a trophy with Brighton, which is why he has extended his contract to 2029. “When I see the team now, they are so into it, they are so committed to it.” He just wouldn’t say when. “Will it be this season? I don’t know. Will it be next season? I don’t know.” Beyond that, he tries not to give it much attention. “These kinds of questions, we can answer them one day.”

#889. How to become a football referee

Honestly, for me it's one of the most rewarding things I've probably ever done. You find so much more out about yourself that you probably never knew.

Louise Thompson, women's referee pathway officer for the Irish Football Association, international FIFA referee, and PremierLeague referee in Northern Ireland.

What does a women's referee pathway officer do?

Looking after female referees within Northern Ireland, trying to recruit, retain and give them experience within their games to pushthrough into top level refereeing.

What kind of training do you give to aspiring referees?

So from going through recruitment courses first of all, and then we do the beginners course with referees, just giving them all of the Laws of the Game knowledge, then we will also do a practical part of that course where they go onto the pitch and we'll go through scenarios, positioning, things around free kick management for example, other set pieces likecorners, penalty setup, what you do as a referee day to day, even pre match stuff as well, so when you arrive at the grounds, how you check the pitch, check all the equipment is there, how you would interact with players, coaches and then just again, maybe createlike a role play sort of environment so that they know that they're not going totally blind into that sort of situation.

Have you always been passionate about football?

Football was a passion of mine, even when I was younger, primary school age, we just didn't have very many female teams, so it normally meant playing with the boys and the boys teams and stuff up until I was about 14, which was the minimum age here you can join senior ladies football team, which is what I did, and played there for 14 years at a club here locally, including up until the Women's Premiership, so it was great to be involved in football, but I always loved watching football, playing football, anything to do with football, I was always there and interested.

How did you go from playing football to being a referee?

Becoming a referee for me sort of happened by chance to be honest. It was during a game, one time I got an injury, quite a bad injury to my knee and then I had seen luckily that the referee course was being advertised. So I signed up for it, but I also signed up for a coaching course pretty much at the same time, maybe about six weeks apart. I wasnât really sure which role I wanted to follow, but over that winter I had been pushed into refereeing a wee bit and said sure, why not, Iâll give it a go, it'd be a bit of extra fitness before my season restarts, and then just fell in love with it from there and never looked back.

What subjects did you study at school and university?

Coming through school I always picked PE, so I did my GCSE PE and then I also did A-level PE and then when I went onto university,I had the sport and exercise science as well within that, so I think it gives you a good understanding of obviously how your body works, and your plan and training, stuff like that as well so you know when you're working nutrition wise, things that you need to know,especially as you reach the top level, just to make sure that you're getting the most out of your body.

What are your top tips for becoming a referee?

I would say definitely give it a try for sure. You never know until you do it. I think even when I was a player, I probably never imaginedthat I would be a referee and that I would even achieve and have experienced what Iâve been able to experience. So you never knowuntil you give it a go, but it's also about probably pushing yourself out of your comfort zone, being comfortable with being uncomfortable in situations like that. It's maybe not always as bad as it probably seems it's going to be. There's probably a lot more stigma around being a referee - who wants to be a referee? - but honestly for me, it's one of the most rewarding things I've probably ever done.

With a lifelong love of football, Louise Thompson followed her passion for the game, first as a player and now as a referee. As well as refereeing Fifa and NIFL Premiership matches, she also works for the Irish Football Association as the women's referee pathway officer, recruiting and developing up-and-coming female refs.

Louise Thompson on refereeing the Women's Irish Cup final.

If you're interested in becoming a referee, it's something you can get involved with from a young age through local referee courses. The minimum age to become a qualified referee varies depending on where in the UK you live:

In her role as a women's referee pathway officer, Louise oversees new referees right from the initial recruitment courses stage: "We then do the beginners' course with referees, giving them all of the Laws of the Game knowledge," she says. "We also do a hands-on part of that course where they go onto the pitch and we go through different scenariosâ¦ exactly what you do as a referee, and day-to-day practical stuff as wellâ¦ The idea is to give them all the basics and fundamentals before they go into a game so that they're prepared."

All four UK nations have established pathways for referee development and progression. Starting out at grassroots level, it's possible to progress all the way to Fifa!

Louise's first games were youth games: "I still remember my first game to this day," she says. "It was an under-13 game, and I was definitely the most nervous person on the pitch." She explains: "Over time, you'll get mentors who will come and watch you, give you advice, give you feedback" which will help you to progress to higher levels of the game.

As well as PE, Louise has found that languages are really helpful in this line of work, "especially when you're dealing with a lot of international games and people coming along," she says. "If you can learn some languages, it's very, very useful."

You could get into this role by training with a professional body.

Sources: National Careers Service, GOV.UK, FA, IFA, SFA, and FAW.

#888. Championship roundup: Strelec sends Middlesbrough top; 10-man Stoke go second

Boro beat Bristol City 2-0; Stoke 1-0 Birmingham

Scott Parker still winless as West Ham held by Preston

Middlesbrough scored a goal either side of half-time to climb to the top of the Championship with a 2-0 win that piled further pressure on the Bristol City manager Michael Skubala.

Adilson Malanda’s header five minutes before half-time was followed by David Strelec’s finish in the 54th minute to secure victory. The three points were effectively secured before Middlesbrough head coach Kim Hellberg introduced the division’s top scorer, Will Lankshear, for the final 14 minutes from the bench after injury. Defeat heightened the frustrations being felt by Bristol City, who have won just one of their last eight matches, as they dropped to 18th.

Hellberg later called Strelec “a brilliant human being” after the Slovakia striker’s first goal since May. “It was a massive moment for David. He has been very good since coming back, he’s shown how good he is in these two games. That goal was a beautiful team goal and he is a top player – you could see how happy he was.”

George Hirst scored the only goal as 10-man Stoke moved into the automatic promotion places with a 1-0 victory against Birmingham. Hirst broke the deadlock in the early stages of the second half before Luca Bombino was shown a second yellow card for the hosts in the 63rd minute. The two teams were level on points at the start of the day, with both having won their last three games, but it was Stoke who prevailed as Hirst scored for the first time since early September.

Adam Armstrong scored his fourth goal in five games and Rafiki Saïd his first for the club as Wolves beat Charlton 2-1 at Molineux. The dominant hosts put their first-half frustrations behind them to score twice in four minutes shortly after the break – both set up by Matheus Mané – before Matty Godden’s 81st-minute consolation rattled a few home nerves. Victory extended Wolves’ unbeaten run to seven games.

Ashley Williams began life as Swansea’s interim head coach with a draw against the club who showed him the door as a 16-year-old 25 years ago. West Brom led twice through goals from Isaac Price and Rabby Nzingoula, but Swansea levelled each time thanks to Moussa Yeo and Elijah Just. All the goals came in an eventful first half, with the crucial moment being a penalty save by the Swansea goalkeeper Lawrence Vigouroux to deny Price.

Stockport took over top spot in League One with a 3-0 victory away at Cambridge. Second-half efforts from Oliver Norwood and Ethan Ennis and an own goal from Gassan Ahadme sent County three points clear of Huddersfield, who lost by the same scoreline against Leicester, with Louis Page netting the only goal.

Oxford are level on points with the Terriers after dramatically beating nine-man Wycombe 4-3. Wanderers led 3-0 but Dan Casey and Luke Leahy both saw red in the second half, and Gatlin O’Donkor’s goal five minutes into injury time completed the comeback.

A Nahki Wells double helped in-form Luton come from behind to beat Burton 2-1 while a very late goal from Sean Grehan helped Doncaster draw 2-2 against high-flying Bradford. Managerless Blackpool were beaten 2-1 by Wigan following Ian Evatt’s sacking and Peterborough beat Plymouth 2-0. There was a notable away victory for struggling Bromley against Reading, Victor Adeboyejo scoring the only goal, while Leyton Orient dispatched AFC Wimbledon 4-1. PA

Tonda Eckert urged Cyle Larin to keep channelling his inner Robert Lewandowski after his goal helped Southampton to a 2-0 victory against Derby. The Canada forward bundled in his eighth goal of the season on his return from a hamstring injury before Divin Mubama settled the contest in stoppage time.

Eckert who crossed paths with Poland great Lewandowski when coaching at Bayern Munich, said: “I think it was an unbelievable finish. Those are the finishes you can’t teach a striker. You have that in your blood. I think Lewandowski said once that if the manager tells you how to move in the box as a No 9 you should do your own thing. Larin knows what to do in the box, there is nothing to tell him.”

Alex Neil fumed at what he called “over-zealous” officiating in Millwall’s 1-0 loss against QPR. While Neil had no complaints about the red card shown to left-back Zak Sturge after just 15 minutes, he took issue with the punishments meted out to him and his backroom staff. The Scot was shown a yellow card following an altercation with the QPR forward Paul Smyth, with his assistant Martin Canning also being booked later on after the goalkeeping coach, Dean Thornton, had been sent from the dugout. Nicolas Madsen’s goal proved decisive at The Den as QPR won away from home for the first time since August and inflicted a third straight defeat on Millwall.

Neil said: “I’ve been coaching for well over a decade at this level and I’ve been booked less than a handful of times. Any time we spoke to the fourth official, he was dishing out bookings like confetti.”

Sheffield United returned to winning ways as they breezed past struggling Watford with a 4-0 victory at Bramall Lane. Two early Ben Brereton Díaz goals and second-half strikes from Jordan Ayew and Sydie Peck sealed a win that was all too easy for the hosts. It was a feisty affair, with referee Tim Robinson handing out 13 yellow cards – much to the disapproval of both sets of fans.

Norwich came from behind to beat Cardiff 2-1 and make it five successive league wins. Yousef Salech put Cardiff ahead three minutes into the second half but the hosts quickly regrouped and were back on level terms on 62 minutes when the in-form Paris Maghoma curled in from just outside the area. The winner arrived six minutes later when Mathias Kvistgaarden’s penalty was saved by Nathan Trott but the Danish striker reacted quickly to stab home the rebound.

League Two leaders Salford held on to a 1-1 draw against Accrington despite being reduced to nine men. All the action came in the second half, with Elliot Bonds putting Salford ahead just after Daniel Udoh had been sent off. Donald Love equalised for Stanley before Bonds also saw red.

Aaron Lewis scored twice as Newport piled the pressure on Ian Holloway with a 2-0 win against Swindon at Rodney Parade. It was a 10th defeat in the last 15 games in all competitions for the visitors.

Barnet closed the gap to four points with two games in hand thanks to a 2-1 victory over Port Vale. Onel Hernández opened the scoring for Vale but was later sent off and Tom Knowles netted what proved to be the winner.

Dylan Duffy scored twice as third-placed Chesterfield defeated Shrewsbury 4-1 while Grimsby and York were both held to goalless draws. A more dramatic draw saw sixth-placed Crewe held 3-3 by Gillingham, with veteran Garath McCleary scoring an injury-time equaliser. Bottom side Crawley claimed their first home win in the league, beating Fleetwood 2-1, but fellow strugglers Rochdale lost a topsy-turvy encounter 3-2 to Northampton. PA

Scott Parker’s stuttering start as West Ham manager continued in his first match at the London Stadium as bottom club Preston battled their way to a 1-1 draw. Parker is yet to taste victory in three games since he returned to the club. After Konstantinos Mavropanos headed home on the hour to cancel out Liam Lindsay’s early goal for the visitors, it seemed that West Ham’s attacking power would force a victory to keep pace in the promotion race. Instead, despite having 27 efforts on goal, they could not break Preston’s resistance and are now winless in their past five games.

Parker said: “I got here really early today and I had a vision of ending the day with three points and a brilliant performance. I got the brilliant performance, but not the three points, so in that sense, I am devastated. But with a rational head, there were a lot of good things, and if we played that game a hundred times, we would win every other time.”

Sam Dalby’s fine effort cancelled out Josh Murphy’s powerful header as Bolton held Portsmouth to an entertaining 1-1 draw, while George Thomason struck a late winner as Wrexham secured a welcome 1-0 victory at Lincoln. It was a first away league victory for Phil Parkinson’s side since the start of September when they beat Millwall 2-0.

#887. 'My job combines my passion for gaming and football'

Working on one of the world's biggest football video games is the perfect combination of my two biggest passions, gaming and football.

I'm CJ Ramson. I work on the creation of football video games. I work on Football Manager as an associate QA manager. QA stands for quality assurance.

We're the ones that test the game. We make sure everything works, and we work closely with the developers to try and make the most realistic simulation of football.

Growing up, I loved football, whether that was playing football or playing football video games with my friends. I'd always be doing one or the other. With the video games, the thing that really drew me to them was I've always been into the tactical side of the game, either being able to control the players or create your own tactics.

So a typical day for us, we'll get a new build in from the developers. We'll test it as a QA team, and we'll look for either bugsor ways that we can improve the game. That can be anything from the runs that players make, to decisions they make on the ball, what the team instructions and tactics do. So there's a lot of areas for us to cover. Our final goal is to make it as realistic to real football as possible.

So even though my background was in coaching, there was a lot of transferable skills that I learned and developed through my time coaching that I managed to transfer into this.
